FINANCE, TRADE AND ECONOMIC AFFAIRS SUGGESTED EXPANSION OF COMMITTEE'S REFERENCE-MOTION UNDER S.O. 43
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, the headlong rush to Canadianize the oil industry and indeed somehow every other industry in the country has resulted in a massive outflow of Canadian capital to the United States and elsewhere. This capital outflow has caused massive foreign borrowing at rates running as high as 2.5 per cent and today 5 per cent above American rates. I therefore move, seconded by the hon. member for Parry Sound-Muskoka (Mr. Darling):
That this House directs that while the Standing Committee on Finance, Trade and Economic Affairs is studying the profits and interest concerns of banks, the reference be extended to include an examination of how the National Energy Program, the Foreign Investment Review Agency and the bills now before the House that militate against foreign investment have contributed to the excessively high interest rates in Canada.

subsubtopic: STATEMENTS MADE BY UNITED STATES AMBASSADOR TO CANADA-MOTION UNDER S.O. 43
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I rise under the provisions of Standing Order 43 on a matter of urgent and pressing necessity. On Saturday in Vancouver, and in Calgary on Monday, the United States Ambassador to Canada, Mr. Paul Robinson, in public addresses called on the Canadian government to buy warships, send another brigade of Canadian troops to Europe, purchase missiles for the F-18 fighter aircraft, and increase this country's defence budget beyond the 18 per cent per year planned for the next two years. This is unsolicited advice on the spending of taxpayers' money and a clear interference in Canadian affairs and policy making by the representative of the United States government. In light of the government's investigation of Sir John Ford's mild comments last year on the Constitution, comments that were not even made in public,
I move, seconded by the hon. member for Skeena (Mr. Fulton):
That this House condemns the direct interference in Canadian affairs by the U.S. Ambassador and calls on the Secretary of State for External Affairs to ask the ambassador for an explanation of his behaviour and public remarks in Vancouver and Calgary, and that he protest to Washington this interference in Canadian affairs by its envoy.

subsubtopic: PENALTIES IMPOSED FOR PREPAYMENT OF MORTGAGES- MOTION UNDER S.O. 43
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I rise under the provisions of Standing Order 43 on a matter of urgent and pressing necessity. In view of the fact that most banks and financial institutions impose substantive penalties for the early retirement or prepayment of mortgages and short-term loans, and in light of the fact that this constitutes usury of the highest sort in today's financial climate, I therefore move, seconded by the hon. member for Hamilton West (Mr. Hudecki):
That the Minister of Finance immediately undertake such legislative or regulatory action as may be necessary to remove or restrain substantively the imposition of penalties for the retirement or prepayment of home mortgages and short-term loans by banks and financial institutions.

speechtext:
Madam Speaker, it has been reported that it could cost the government $100 million a year to subsidize the domestic price of barley in eastern Canada under the corn competitive pricing formula. That the Minister of Agriculture immediately abolish the corn competitive formula pricing arrangement and allow feed grains sold in Canada to be priced at the going export rate.

subsubtopic: EFFECT OF HIGH INTEREST RATES ON INFLATION
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, my question is directed to the Minister of State for Finance. He will know that the recent report of the Conference Board of Canada indicated that, as a result of the high interest rate policy of the federal government, rates of unemployment will continue to increase, consumer spending will decrease, and business investment will continue to decrease in Canada for the rest of 1982, well into 1983, and perhaps beyond that. Is the government's high interest rate policy intended eventually to reduce the rate of inflation in the country?
[ Translation]

subsubtopic: EFFECT OF HIGH INTEREST RATES ON INFLATION
speechtext: Madam Speaker, I may remind the hon. member that the views expressed by the Conference Board are a little more complex than the simplified version he had to give because of the nature of the question period. Furthermore, the government is not pursuing a high interest rate policy; the hon. member should understand that interest rates in Canada are high because of very strong inflationary pressures. In addition, as a result of the dependence of our economy on the economies of our trading partners, high interest rates prevailing elsewhere affect our economy as well. If the hon. member supports the government's anti-inflationary policy and inflationary pressures continue to decline, he will find the Conference Board agreeing that interest rates will go down. Another conclusion is that this year will be seen as a period of transition to 1983, when an upswing in investment is expected, with more jobs and thus a drop in the unemployment rate.

subsubtopic: EFFECT OF HIGH INTEREST RATES ON INFLATION
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subtopic: QUERY RESPECTING POSSIBLE EFFECT OF INCREASED PRODUCTIVITY
QUERY RESPECTING POSSIBLE EFFECT OF INCREASED PRODUCTIVITY
speechtext: Madam Speaker, on a number of occasions the Minister of Finance has indicated that the present monetary policy pursued by the government is intended to be a major step in the fight against inflation. If inflation is defined as when there are too many dollars chasing too few products, or when spending increases more rapidly than production, would the minister agree that while Canada and other nations have been attempting to reduce inflation by reducing spending, another approach to combating inflation would be to increase significantly the amount of production in the country?

subtopic: QUERY RESPECTING POSSIBLE EFFECT OF INCREASED PRODUCTIVITY
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, in his first question the hon. member referred specifically to the Conference Board, and I am going to refer him to the Conference Board. There he will find the
April 22, 1982

answer to his question, since the Board is advising the government to maintain its policy of restraint as expressed in the fiscal plan set forth in the budget, and it is by maintaining the restrictions in the government's fiscal plan that the fight against inflation can be made yet more effective so that it will remove uncertainty among investors, thus increasing investment and creating jobs and consequently bringing about a drop in both the unemployment rate and our interest rates.

Madam Speaker, despite the minister's response and his continual reference to the Conference Board of Canada, while other countries are pursuing a monetary policy in their efforts to reduce inflation a country such as Canada has another alternative, and that is to increase production in the country. Why is the government not taking immediate steps to reduce the idle capacity in our economy which currently stands at 25 per cent, and refusing to require corporations like Toyota and Honda to source and assemble automobiles which they sell in the country, right here in Canada?

Madam Speaker, as far as the question about negotiations with other countries on automobile manufacturing is concerned, the minister responsible for International Trade is always available to answer this type of question. Regarding the general economic situation and our production capacity, I have already made it clear to the hon. member that as long as we have a climate of uncertainty which is, in fact, caused by high interest rates, investment will drop and consumer spending and consumer demand will drop as well, so that idle production capacity is due to this climate of uncertainty. If we really want consumer demand to pick up, we must get rid of the uncertainty caused by high inflation rates.

speechtext:
Madam Speaker, my question is for the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources. The minister will know that my colleagues from Newfoundland and Nova Scotia have continually questioned the government with respect to the Ocean Ranger tragedy. Last evening, nine weeks from the date of the tragedy, Canadians watched a television news report from the United States covering the U.S. Coast Guard hearings in Boston. This House welcomes
Oral Questions
their concern, but I suggest to the minister that Canadians find it offensive that Americans have acted promptly to determine why so many Canadians lost their lives when the Canadian inquiry will not even start until October. Does the minister not find that delay to be unconscionable and offensive?

speakeroldname: Hon. Marc Lalonde (Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources):
speakerposition: Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources
subsubtopic: SINKING OF "OCEAN RANGER"-INVESTIGATION BY UNITED STATES AUTHORITIES
speechtext: Madam Speaker, the government of Newfoundland and the Government of Canada have set up a joint royal commission to investigate this tragedy. This has been agreed to by both governments and supported by all parties in this House. The royal commission is chaired by the Chief Justice of Newfoundland, accompanied by five prominent Newfoundlanders. At the present time the commission is at work gathering information and conducting studies. As a matter of fact one member of the commission is present at the hearings in Boston. I would suggest to my hon. friend that it is not appropriate to ask me to reflect upon the members of such a prominent commission.

speakerposition: Deputy House Leader of the Official Opposition; Progressive Conservative Party Deputy House Leader
speechtext: Madam Speaker, while Canadians are obtaining offices and hiring staff, the Americans have been able to get their inquiry under way. Was there ever any attempt to hold a joint inquiry with the U.S. Coast Guard so this matter could be acted upon immediately, since there will be lives at risk at sea next winter and the commission will not even be off the ground?

speakeroldname: Hon. Marc Lalonde (Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources):
speakerposition: Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources
speechtext: Madam Speaker, first, it has been determined that there will be full co-operation between the Canadian and the United States governments in this regard. Any information that we have is accessible to our American friends, and vice versa. As far as the internal investigation by the American Coastguard is concerned, it is being followed very closely and, obviously, when it comes up with recommendations they will be public and it will be up to the government to make sure that those recommendations which we find acceptable are put into effect without having to wait for the report from the royal commission. But again, our royal commission is one with a broad mandate and it wants to carry out a very full investigation, not only of the Ocean Ranger tragedy but also of practices aboard drilling rigs and platforms offshore. I think we should give that commission the necessary time to do its work.

Is it the policy of the Canadian National Railways to force (a) supervisory personnel into early retirement (b) senior supervisory personnel to accept positions of lower rating until their retirement?

speakeroldname: Mr. Jesse P. Flis (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Transport):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Transport
speechtext:
The management of Canadian National Railways advises as follows:
(a)	No. However, if an employee's job is redundant due to technological, organizational, or operational changes; changes in administrative procedures, services, or volume of business; or budget requirements; and such employee cannot be fitted into another position, then the employee may apply for early retirement.
(b)	In some circumstances, a senior supervisory position may become redundant due to the reasons mentioned above and the officer could elect to accept an alternative position, if available. In such cases the employee's pay, is ordinarily held at the same rate as that prior to the person's accepting a lower alternative position.

The House resumed, from Wednesday, April 21, consideration of the motion of Mr. Lalonde that Bill C-103, to amend
Energy Administration Act
the Petroleum Administration Act and to enact provisions related thereto, be read the second time and referred to the Standing Committee on Energy Legislation.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: The hon. member for Vancouver-Kings-way (Mr. Waddell).

Madam Speaker,
I thought we were starting debate on Bill C-103.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: Does the hon. member seek the floor? He has it.

Madam Speaker, at the end of the sitting the other day the hon. member for Calgary Centre (Mr. Andre) was speaking. I believe he was stopped in the middle of his speech and he has not risen to continue speaking. If he is not going to continue then I am rising as the first speaker.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: The hon. member has the floor.

I rise to speak on this bill which was to be named the Petroleum Administration Act but will now be renamed the energy administration act. It is a bill that deals with energy taxation in Canada and it should really be renamed the "mugging of the consumers act" or perhaps even the "legislation of thievery at the gas pump act".
You are absolutely right.

It robs and plunders the poor Canadian consumer. It loots the consumer at the gas pump. That is what the bill does and we should make no mistake about that.
While the daily press hung on every moment of the bellringing, since we started the energy debate there has been very little interest in it and very few news stories. That is too bad because both the Conservative party and the New Democratic Party have offered some telling points about the whole energy scheme and the Canadianization of the industry and will make in this debate today some comments about taxation. The government has not shown much interest and has put up few speakers in reply. I am sorry that press reporters and commentators have not given the subject the kind of in-depth analysis it deserves.
These bills will affect Canadians in crucial ways and in many respects will change the whole energy industry and the country in very important ways. This is not an energy security bill; it is a taxation bill which will sock it to the Canadian consumer and refill the coffers of the government. Most of the money will go to a government that negligently emptied its coffers through its mismanagement and incompetence.
You put them in.
Let me deal with that matter of putting the government in. It was the Canadian people who put it in, and now the Canadian people have to judge-

You aided and abetted them.

April 22, 1982
Energy Administration Act

-whether it is living up to the promises it made. In fact, it is following the Conservative energy policy, which we objected to in the first place, of high taxation at the pumps. That is what the Conservative energy policy was.
It was 18 cents at the pumps.
Let us make no mistake about that. My friend to my right will have an opportunity to speak on this and I want to hear them.
They will talk sense.
Let us make it quite clear that if you analyse what the Clark government policy was-
It was 18 cents.

-and what the Crosbie budget was, you will find that there were to be dramatic increases in energy prices over the third, fourth and fifth year of that so-called agreement with Alberta. The energy prices that the Conservatives were going to bring in were higher than those proposed by the Liberal government. I think the Canadian consumer is at the point of saying "a plague on both their houses".
These tax measures are not the type that the New Democratic Party believes in. They are something like a sales tax which is a regressive tax. Low income people, poor people, ordinary people have to spend more of their incomes on the necessities of life, such as food, lodging, heat, light and transportation, than people who have more money. I will go into more detail on these taxes that the government proposes through this bill and our criticism of them in a few minutes.
These taxes are already hurting the ordinary person and they are going to hurt more. People are asking why we have to pay more for gasoline here than we do across the border from Vancouver or Windsor. Well they should ask, because I think people feel that this thievery I spoke of is compounded by two things. First of all, there was a shameless promise in the last election by this government, supposedly to appeal to Ontario and eastern Canadian voters where apparently elections are won or lost-southern Ontario to be specific-that somehow the Liberal Party had the key to keeping energy prices low. I think it is pretty clear now that was not exactly what they had in mind. They certainly have not done it.
The second reason I think people are upset is that these prices are going up at the same time as the government proposes to give away an unprecedented amount of money to the oil industries. You know the oil industry, Mr. Speaker: "Give us more money and we will find more oil." Of course, when we do that they then want to export the oil. That has been the historical pattern in Canada and Canadians know it.
If you were to ask the person on the street they would say yes, we have given the industry a lot of money and they end up pressuring for exports, and an acquiescent National Energy Board and government allow the exports. We have just passed
a bill which authorizes $6.5 billion in PIP grants to the oil industry. I know there are certain segments in the industry, the small producers, who are now hurting and both I and my party have some sympathy for them. But in general this industry is controlled by the multinationals; by Exxon of New York, the largest company in the world, Royal Dutch Shell, and Texaco and Gulf of the United States. Some of that $6.5 billion will go to them.
That money, Mr. Speaker, is coming out of the pockets of Canadian consumers. It goes back to the government and then to the oil companies. This is the Liberal idea; they call it recycling.
NDP socialism.
That is not NDP socialism. .
What are they doing in Saskatchewan?

When the member gives me a chance I will point out how we will do it. It is Liberal Canadianization, Mr. Speaker, and I invite the hon. member to study the speeches of his own energy critic so that he can understand what that is. This Canadianization program, which involves taking money from us at the pumps and giving it back to the oil companies by way of PIP grants, is a sham and a fraud. It is a legal means of holding up the Canadian consumer at the pump and on his heating bill. There are alternatives and I hope in the course of my speech to point them out.
This act, Mr. Speaker, does essentially six things. It raises the oil export charge ceiling and confirms the charges imposed since May, 1979. It gives authority to turn over 50 per cent of the resulting revenue to the producing provinces. Secondly, it establishes a transportation fuel compensation recovery charge. Third, it implements changes to the petroleum compensation charge, thereby enabling the implementation of a blended price system for oil. Fourth, it establishes the authority for and termination of a special compensation charge relating to the cut-off of Alberta oil last year. Fifth, it ends the petroleum compensation board and continues and expands its function in the Department of Energy, Mines and Resources. Sixth, it establishes the Canadian ownership special charge and the Canadian ownership account.
The operative word in those six items is the word "charge". We are going to be charged at the gas pump, on our heating bills, and we are going to be charged for planning. I now want to analyse each one of these charges and give the NDP position on them, and I invite my friend over there from Alberta to listen and give a reasoned response. I know that is asking a lot of him, but he just might rise to the occasion.
Firstly, the petroleum compensation charge is a mechanism whereby the blended price of oil is developed. It is a charge at the pump and is used to compensate refiners who import more expensive foreign oil. We have to import oil because we are self-sufficient in all forms of energy except oil. The question, I suppose, is why? The reason is that in the early 1970s we
April 22, 1982

exported one-half of our daily production, which was then called surplus. The oil industry told the National Energy Board, which in turn told the Government of Canada, that we had enough oil for 300 years. Then the OPEC crisis came along, and the oil industry then said: "Oh, we have enough oil for 11 years." They misled the Government of Canada, and now today we have all those television ads by oil company executives saying: "Trust us, we will look after you." The Canadian people do not believe that because they have been burned already, and every time they go to the pumps and pay this compensation charge they should keep that in mind.
The pattern, Mr. Speaker, and it is an historical one, is simple. The industry says we have a shortage, we need more money. They are given tax advantages like the super depletion allowance, they are given $6.5 billion in grants, and then they say we have lots of oil and now we have to export it. They then lobby the government and the government allows exports. We then have a shortage again, and how do you get rid of the shortage? You guessed it: we need more grants, more allowances. That is the pattern and it has to stop. If we were the Government of Canada we would stop it. We would stop taking money out of the consumer's pocket and recycling it back to the industry. The system is stupid, it makes no sense and has to be changed. That is the reason we must import foreign oil and pay for it.
Certain refiners in Canada are currently being overcompensated anywhere from $7 to $12 a barrel because they are buying cheaper oil on the spot market, whereas the compensation under this legislation and the existing system is based on the average world price of oil landed in Montreal. While the payments may average out for the industry as a whole, nevertheless certain refiners are receiving a windfall. There should be a more accurate system of calculating the compensation, or paying additional compensation where needed. In other words, we must compensate refiners for their actual costs.
I was looking at an article printed in "Quorum" and appearing in various newspapers. The article was written by W.A. Wilson. The heading of his article reads:"Oil subsidy should draw Tory, NDP wrath." I wonder whether this Mr. Wilson exists. I wonder where he lives. In the House of Commons for the last three weeks, the hon. member for Calgary West (Mr. Hawkes), myself and several other Conservative members have been asking questions in the House of Commons and have been before the Standing Committee on Public Accounts dealing precisely with this question. It makes me wonder where the journalists are these days when it comes to analysing issues.
This matter has been raised in the House of Commons. The government has been pressed on this. Therefore, I do not know where Mr. Wilson gets his information. Perhaps he is not around here in Ottawa and does not follow what happens in the House of Commons. If he were here, Mr. Wilson would know that the charge allows some refiners to buy foreign oil for less than the cost of Alberta oil. That is what the opposition has been saying. This procedure has resulted in shut-in oil
Energy Administration Act
production of 50,000 barrels per day in western Canada. That amount of shut-in oil could rise to 300,000 barrels per day. I know about this because I visited Saskatchewan recently. I talked with people in Saskatchewan and with the Saskatchewan government, who have brought pressure to bear on Ottawa to change the system of the petroleum compensation charge so there would not be shut-in oil in Saskatchewan. Crudely put-and pardon the pun, Mr. Speaker-this petroleum compensation system is really crazy. So far the government has asked only eastern refiners to give preference to western Canadian oil. The government has not shown any teeth on this.
Last night hon. members heard the Conservative critic, the hon. member for Calgary Centre, rant and rave about many things. He talked about the Western Canada Concept which causes people in the west a great deal of difficulty. I suggest hon. members opposite take a close look at this very legitimate grievance of western oil producers and western business. Frankly, I think the minister could react much more strongly on this issue.
I think the principal causes of the problem are twofold. First, there has been a substantial decline in oil consumption in Canada as well as in the United States. Second, there has been a signing of long-term contracts with the federal government's encouragement during the period of Lougheed's oil cutback. In effect, this deal has now boomeranged on the province of Alberta, of which some people think the minister is taking advantage. It is sort of "Lalonde's revenge", if you like. The deal also resulted in the difficulties out west and there is a great deal of pressure both on the minister of energy here and the minister of energy in Alberta to do something about them.
Those are probably the reasons we are into the shut-in oil situation. There will be pressure to alleviate the shut-in problem by exporting western Canadian light crude. There will be pressure in western Canada to export. The government should resist that pressure. Instead, it should take steps to make sure that Canadian oil is used in place of imported oil because that makes better sense. How do we do that? We could lower the petroleum compensation charge so there is more incentive to use Canadian crude oil. This would also result in cheaper gasoline at the pump. We could expand the capacity of the present transCanada pipeline system to allow more western oil to reach eastern markets. This suggestion would fit in with the long-term plan to bring in Beaufort Sea oil by pipeline to eastern markets.
The Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Lalonde) was quoted in Ottawa's paper, The Citizen. The article's heading says: "Lalonde blames separatism on Western politicians". The minister of energy, from a west end Montreal riding, I understand, is reported to have said that western politicians are distorting facts and in fact not doing their job correctly. In spite of some early provocation today, I have not stood up and ranted and raved in any way. I have tried to analyse this petroleum compensation charge and I have set out

April 22, 1982
Energy Administration Act
some concrete suggestions for improvement. You cannot say that western politicians are not doing their job. I just heard one of my constituents in the gallery agreeing with me.
The issue is costly to consumers. The present rate of compensation to importers is $17.32 per barrel. Who is paying that amount? The Canadian consumer, of course. The present petroleum compensation charge per barrel of oil consumed in Canada is $6.30. This means the consumer is paying 18 cents per gallon of gasoline for this charge. The cost of compensating purchases of foreign oil appears as appropriations in the Main Estimates. I invite members to look them. If hon. members do that, they will see that in the period 1980 to 1981, the amount set out is $3.16 billion; in the period 1981 to 1982, the amount is $5.16 billion; and the amount budgeted for 1982 to 1983 is $2.97 billion. That money does not come from thin air. It comes from the Canadian consumer who pays it at the gas pump. It comes from Canadian consumers when they pay their heating bills.
This is a bad situation and it must be changed. On behalf of the New Democratic Party, I will propose amendments at the appropriate stage to deal with this problem. Let not Mr. Wilson and his colleagues say that opposition politicians are not prepared to deal with the problem. Let not the minister of energy say that western politicians do not take their duty to bring concrete suggestions to this government seriously. For a change, let this government listen and bring in some of these changes.
The second charge is the transportation fuel compensation recovery charge. I know that this is a very difficult bill and I am trying to go through it to make everything as simple as I can in order to explain to the Canadian people who are watching and listening to us throughout the country what these things mean. They are understandable. I explained the petroleum compensation charge because we have to import foreign oil. I explained that we had to import foreign oil because we exported all our oil years ago. I have told the people how much all this costs, but I think people know that because they pay for it at the gas pump every three or four days.
What about the transportation fuel compensation recovery charge? That is a real mouthful, Mr. Speaker. On behalf of our party we object to this recovery charge being applied at this time. It is a transportation charge on aircraft, ships and so on. It should not be applied to the marine and shipping industry in Canada at this time. We advocate that Canadian water carriers be exempted from this charge since rail, air and road transportation in many ways is also exempted. The charge would bring fuel prices to world levels. Exemptions should remain until the government is committed to developing a Canadian flag merchant marine, until the government requires a minimum of 40 per cent of our international trade be carried in Canadian vessels and until shipping between Canadian ports is restricted to Canadian vessels.
We say the charge on Canadian vessels is discriminatory. In other words it should not apply to Canadian ships. Also that clause of the bill allows the federal government to set prices for
offshore oil and oil in the territories. We believe this should be done by negotiation with the concerned territorial and provincial governments, with a view to arriving at revenue-sharing agreements as was done with western provinces.
The Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) appears to have rejected co-operative federalism. He said recently that co-operative federalism was dead. It was a tragic mistake for the country and for the Liberal Party, the party of Pearson and of cooperative federalism. As he throws co-operative federalism out of the window, I suggest he risks ultimately throwing his own party out of the window. The Liberal Party has chosen to be a federal party, simply a national party, only interested in winning power on the national level. The Liberal Party appears to be dead in the west. As the Prime Minister picks fights with more and more provinces and throws out co-operative federalism, he runs the real risk of ultimately destroying any power base his party might have. That is not my problem; it is the problem of the party opposite and of the country.
Canadians are fed up with provincial premiers bashing the federal government and the Prime Minister bashing provincial premiers. If there is any message in the Prime Minister's confrontation with Mr. Levesque in terms of the reaction of Canadians, it is that they would like both of them to cool it. It affects the energy field. We recall that when we debated the Petroleum Administration Act in the House, the federal government imposed an oil price on Alberta before reaching an agreement with the province. Under the terms of the act as it then was, we were allowed a six-day debate. It was a good debate, but the problem was that the government did not listen to what opposition members said. If it had, it would have understood before making the deal with Alberta that there was a problem with some small oil and gas companies and with respect to the position taken by Canadian consumers. The clause in the bill which allows the government to set prices unilaterally for offshore and the north should not be implemented. Prices should be set after consultation with offshore provinces and the two territorial governments. I propose to bring in some amendments to the bill to cover that area.
Clause 16 in effect allows the federal government to set prices unilaterally for crude oil where agreement cannot be reached with the concerned provinces. We agree in principle that the federal government ought to have the final power to do this. I say this as a westerner. I believe in provinces having control of their resources. We have moved to have that included in the Constitution, but for a strategic commodity like energy it makes sense, if ultimately there cannot be an agreement with a province, for the federal government to have the final power.
What did the federal government do in this bill? With Clause 19 on page 12 it removed the opportunity for Parliament to debate such action. Again, this will hurt co-operative federalism. The government does not have any representatives from oil producing areas in the western part of the country. I
April 22, 1982

see the Minister of Employment and Immigration (Mr. Axworthy) entering the Chamber. I am talking about west of the Winnipeg city limits. Since the government has no western representatives, it should be very careful when dealing with gut issues in western Canada. But the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources, who I call the six-foot Napoleon, blames separatism on western Canadian politicians! Clause 19 of this very complicated bill is important in terms of retaining cooperative federalism.
Next I should like to deal with the oil export charge. It was established in 1974 to ensure that when Canadian oil was exported the federal government received the difference between the domestic price and the rapidly rising export price which would have normally accrued to the exporter. The reason for this charge still holds true. There should be no price incentive to export domestic oil while Canada continues to be a net importer of oil. The governments of Alberta and Saskatchewan do not currently share in the export tax revenue, but because the federal government is committed to an equitable revenue-sharing system, the new act gives it authority to offer exporting provinces 50 per cent of the revenue gained through the export charge as of November, 1980. This is an example of co-operative federalism. We have no objection to it and we support it.
Another charge is the special compensation charge. Clause 39 contains a special charge on petroleum products levied from March 31, 1981 to September 21, 1981, to pay for extra imports of oil due to the decision of the Alberta government to cut back oil production during the bitter energy negotiations between the province and the federal government last year. This charge is no longer in effect because of the September, 1981 agreement. Since it is a fait accompli, the fact that it has been removed, we in the New Democratic Party do not have any objection to the clause.
However, I would not want to let the occasion pass without castigating the federal and provincial governments for their intransigence in the negotiations. When one thinks about it, that little example of co-operative federalism between Premier Lougheed and the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources cost Canadian consumers an extra $1.85 per barrel, or 6 cents per gallon, for gasoline over that period. Again, when politicians bash each other, ultimately the poor consumer suffers.
I heard the hon. member for Calgary Centre talk about the Western Canada Concept obtaining support in my province. For example, last night 1,200 people attended a meeting to protest. There are alternatives upon which ordinary Canadians can insist. They can insist upon better government. This unnecessary spat was a poor example of government that ended up costing consumers 6 cents extra per gallon for gasoline. By the way, the total collected by the federal tax was over $460 million. This was $142 million more than needed to pay for the extra imports. Did the government give back the $142 million to Canadian consumers? Obviously it did not. It overcharged us and then pocketed the rest of the money into general revenue, to be used for us but really to be spent on some rather strange things.
Energy Administration Act
The next charge is the Canadian ownership special charge. Revenue from the Canadian ownership special charge and from increases to the natural gas and natural gas liquids excise taxes will accumulate in the Canadian ownership account and be used to increase participation by the federal government in the petroleum industry. As I have said many times in the House, the New Democratic Party believes in government participation in the industry. That is why people like David Lewis and Tommy Douglas who represented this party moved for the establishment of Petro-Canada in the early 1970s. We believe that Petro-Canada must be put in the driver's seat to deal with multinational oil companies. Logic demands that this be done.
I quoted in the House an article by Geoffrey Simson who wrote in The Globe and Mail about the system which exists in Norway. There is no problem in Norway where Statoil is in the driver's seat from where it can direct the industry and its development. This does not preclude private sectors participating in the energy industry, but they are given a clear direction as to what course the industry should follow in order to have energy security and job availability for people in that country.
While Canadians should be pleased to see Petro-Canada signs going up, they should not be misled. As was pointed out to the Standing Committee on Energy Legislation yesterday in questions I put to the vice-president of Petro-Canada as well as to the minister, the number one oil company in Canada is Imperial Oil, which is owned by Exxon in the United States. The number one Canadian oil company is not Petro-Canada, it is Dome Petroleum. Petro-Canada is number five.
We should not be misled because Petro-Canada is not in the driver's seat; nor has the federal government any intention of putting it there. During the committee hearing today I asked the former Canadian ambassador to the United States whether he would confirm what he said in his speech in the United States. Speaking for the Canadian government, he said that it would not make Petro-Canada the dominant player. That is government policy. As a matter of fact, if hon. members review the bill carefully, the Canadian ownership special charge has been reduced from a possible maximum of $4 a barrel to $1.15 a barrel. There have been similar reductions in the natural gas tax maximum.
This is a significant retreat from the October, 1980 budget and the National Energy Program. The government had indicated in both policies that in its pursuit of expanding the role of Petro-Canada or other Crown corporations in the energy field, it was prepared to raise the necessary funds for takeovers by this special levy. Since the levy is at its maximum, it appears there will be no more takeovers in the near future.
Good.

I heard some hon. member to my right say good. Well, if we do not have a takeover now or in the near future, we will never gain control and set a direction for our oil

April 22, 1982
Energy Administration Act
industry in Canada. This Liberal Canadianization program, with its PIP grants, Canadian ownership rates and amendments to the Canada Business Corporations Act, is convoluted, complicated and ultimately unworkable.
The most simple, straightforward and efficient method- and one which Canadians would understand-for accomplishing Canadianization is to use that $6.5 billion which will be given away to take over a major oil company like Imperial Oil. We would then have 50 per cent of the industry under Canadian control. We would not have to wait until 1990.
There is support for this idea. Mr. Robert Laxer of the Committee to Canadianize appeared before the committee this morning and produced a Gallup poll which indicated that 70 per cent of Canadians, I believe, wanted to make Petro-Canada the dominant player in the industry and to take over one of the foreign majors and, as well, to advance the target of 50 per cent Canadian ownership by 1990 to 75 per cent ownership by 1985. The only way to accomplish this is by taking public ownership of one of the majors. A move such as this by the government would be supported by Canadians.
I realize that the government is faced with a Conservative party which literally hates Petro-Canada and wishes to destroy it. This sentiment is quite evident when you listen to Conservative members in committee and in the House. We should continue with the thrust of the National Energy Program and not back off from it as this government is apparently doing. An example of government backing off is shown when it proposes to reduce its original maximum tax of $4 a barrel to $1.15 a barrel.
I will let other members deal with this issue but I would like to make two points in conclusion. I recently spoke to a clothing manufacturer in Vancouver. His clothing prices have not risen recently. I also talked to a small gas producer who told me that his prices have not gone up. Therefore, where is this inflation coming from? Why are the prices going up? The answer is that they are going up through government taxes, which I think is obvious. Statistics Canada recently said that the latest oil price increase was a key reason for another rise in the cost of living. The consumer price index indicated that the cost of energy-related items such as gasoline and home heating fuel rose by 5.4 per cent during March as the impact of the January increase in the wellhead price of crude oil hit at the consumer level. Prices are rising and inflation is increasing because the government is raising these energy taxes so frequently.
I suppose some members could say that you have to collect taxes in order to provide services. The Prime Minister constantly says this to us every time we ask him a question. While it is true that taxes must be collected, there are other means of taxation. A proper proportion of corporate income tax is never really collected from the oil companies. As a matter of fact, an average Canadian family with two children which earns $25,000 pays more in tax in percentage terms than the oil companies do. This situation is scandalous. Collecting taxes at the pump is a regressive form of taxation because it applies to average Canadians who pay a greater proportion of their income for food, heating and transit. That is why these taxes
are unsatisfactory. There are other ways to collect the money. I believe that the Liberal government stands indicted in the eyes of Canadians for having promised cheap energy prices and then delivering an energy pricing regime which is exactly the same as that which the Conservatives were going to introduce.
Finally, I conclude by replying to some of the remarks made by the hon. member for Calgary Centre who is the Conservative energy critic. Incidentally, I notice that hardly any Liberal members have spoken to this energy issue-
[ Translation]
-and especially the francophone members from Quebec! The Quebec members never take part in discussions on energy legislation.

I think that is scandalous. I hope that the Conservative member from Quebec will speak because we never hear from a Quebec member. Are they not interested in this Parliament? We never hear them speak about energy and I suggest that they do so. They are here just to vote, that is all. With the exception of one or two Liberal members, they are not interested or informed.
The hon. member for Calgary Centre spoke of his concern over western separatism. We all share that concern. This country seems to be coming apart in terms of regionalism. However, when I listened to the hon. member, it was like a scene from Macbeth: strutting and fretting his hour upon the stage, signifying nothing. There was much strutting and fretting, but very few positive suggestions.
I am a western MP. I have seen this country and it is a wealthy and magnificent country. It is crazy that this country should break up or that this country should have Quebec separatism or western separatism. It is nonsense. There must be some reason for it. The reason is that we are not getting good government policy. There are better ways of dealing with our differences. There are great things ahead for this country if all the people work together. What a great struggle it would be to patriate our energy industry as we patriated our Constitution! What a magnificent challenge it would be! That is the kind of thing we could do. What do we hear every day? We hear the Conservatives raising arguments to give more money to a basically foreign-controlled industry. We could do it better and more simply. I say to the Canadian people out there that we could take some of the

money that we are about to give away to oil companies through Bill C-103 and use it to put into our own company, Petro-Canada, in which we are all shareholders. On Saturday morning I am going back to my constituency. In my store-front office I see many people with problems. Many are immigrants and most are ordinary people. They are not sophisticated people. Mr. Speaker, this bill proposes that the government should be given the right to increase the price of gasoline at the pump by a very considerable amount, following the increase of 28 cents per gallon at the pump which its taxes have brought about during the past two years. This is a ridiculous proposition. As we all know, during the past year there has been a world overproduction of oil, and this has caused world prices of oil to fall sharply. The taxes which the government has been adding to the price of gasoline at the pump during the past two years were supposed to pay for the increasing subsidy the government has been paying on the one-fifth of our oil requirements which could not be supplied by Canadian sources and must be bought from offshore. The subsidy was necessary so that all Canadians could enjoy the Canadian price. However, if the cost of the foreign oil we are subsidizing is falling, the taxes needed to pay for the subsidy should be decreasing also, not increasing. In other words, the price we pay for gasoline at the pump should be coming down at it has been doing in the United States and in most other countries, not going up.
For the government to seek the right to increase taxes to pay for a subsidy which is decreasing is simply ridiculous and should be refused by every hon. member of this House. I, most certainly, will be voting against this bill.

Mr. Speaker, I want to take this opportunity to make a few points concerning this particular bill. At the outset, I should say that when one looks at the contents of this particular piece of legislation, one immediately finds that it is really not an energy bill or a petroleum administration bill. It is indeed a taxation bill. Quite frankly, all Liberals should hang their heads in shame while asking us to approve this measure, because it could more appropriately be called "an act to facilitate a massive tax grab", rather than a bill aimed at providing energy security.
Energy Administration Act
The bill is entitled, "An Act to Amend the Petroleum Administration Act", and it will have the effect of changing that title to read "The Energy Administration Act". The only thing that is administrative about it is the fact that huge taxes will be collected from the consumers of Canada, many of which are questionable, many of which are unwieldy, and many of which are very damaging and detrimental, not only to the economy but, indeed, to the petroleum industry of Canada as well.
There are essentially six different varieties of confiscation included in this particular measure: an oil export charge; a tax on transportation fuel; a petroleum compensation charge, a levy to a maximum of $ 12 per barrel which will be to cover the import oil compensation; there are provisions for retroactive authority to cover the special compensation charge. The bill covers a tax to fund the Canadian ownership charge. It provides the government authority to amend the pricing terms of the Syncrude agreement. It all amounts to a massive tax rip-off at the expense of the Canadian consumer. It is clearly another of those examples of a dramatic increase in the level of indirect taxation.
The effects of the budget and the provisions enshrined in this piece of legislation will be to double the level of indirect taxation on individual Canadians. It really also demonstrates the stupidity of this government's energy policy when Canadian consumers are being asked to pay taxes of the order of 20 cents to 25 cents a gallon to subsidize oil which is imported at world prices from the OPEC countries, from Saudi Arabia, from Venezuela and Mexico, while western Canadian production is shut in, throwing people out of work, creating bankruptcies, business failures and business cutbacks, causing people to lose their homes and causing communities which have thrived on the vitality of the oil industry in the west to falter.
One must examine this situation in the light of whether it is simply an act of stupidity or whether it is a deliberate attack upon the people of Canada. My colleague suggests that it is malicious. Many people in western Canada firmly believe this is an attack by the federal government on western resources. It is nothing more than a deliberate mischievous attack upon a resource, the economy and the livehlihood of western Canadians. It is drying up economic opportunities which western Canadians felt were on the horizon. The eighties were to have been the decade of tremendous growth, development and opportunity in terms of broadening the economic base and increasing the manufacturing and processing sectors so that more and more Canadians who were born, raised and educated in western Canada could fulfil their potential and their dreams. They could make their homes, establish their businesses and fulfil their careers with a sense of satisfaction and fulfilment.
The deliberate attack by this government in terms of its proposed National Energy Program, taxation policies and budgetary policies enshrined in October, 1980 and November,

1981 have caused a sense of hopelessness and despair, frustration, anger and outrage. This is causing a deep sense of alienation and aggravation in western Canada.

I am pleased that the Minister of Employment and Immigration (Mr. Axworthy) is in the chamber. While his constituency does not penetrate the deep west, as it is in Winnipeg, I am sure he has had reports of what is occurring. I invite him to read the editorial pages and to contact his friends in the Liberal Party and other parties to talk about this very important issue. He is in a position of influence within cabinet. I implore this minister and his colleagues to realize that something must be done in order to remove this kind of feeling, which is taking off like wildfire. It will require more than simply a gesture; it will require some fundamental shifts in government policy. We cannot afford division, discord and disharmony in this country and expect it to function in a way that all regions and all citizens have a similar opportunity to achieve their full potential.
We have a situation where we now import in excess of 500,000 barrels of oil a day at world prices, $40 a barrel. At the same time, we are told that during the month of April something like 300,000 barrels of oil a day will be shut in in the province of Alberta. Simply put, we are buying oil at $40 a barrel from offshore sources and leaving 300,000 barrels of potential oil shut in in the province of Alberta. This would cost the domestic consumer $23.50 a barrel. It simply does not make sense.
We are not asking for a handout. Nor are we asking for a policy that favours the west. We want a commonsense policy. How silly, ridiculous and stupid can this government be? This is simply a matter for good common sense.
In the province of Saskatchewan and in some areas of Alberta heavy oil and low-producing wells are located. I am told that in Saskatchewan there are some 8,500 producing wells, 5,500 of which produce less than 20 barrels a day. We are therefore talking about small amounts from individual oil wells. However, the labour component is very high. The labour component in terms of collection devices, the distribution system, makes this oil production entity very important to western Canada in terms of providing jobs, strengthening the business community and vitalizing it. Those production
facilities are very labour-intensive. That business has literally dried up.
The New Democratic Party supports the general thrust and objectives of the National Energy Program. I find that rather strange. It is the general objectives and thrust of the National Energy Program that have literally destroyed the oil industry in Saskatchewan and virtually destroyed the heavy oil and the industry which produced the very light crude in Alberta.
This is why we do not have on stream a Cold Lake heavy oil facility, a heavy oil upgrading facility onstream in the Lloyd-minister area or an Alsands project onstream. This is because of this government's failure to recognize the realities of the oil industry. There is certainly not much experience in this cabinet in Ottawa with regard to what it takes to make an oil well produce, get the oil out of the ground, refine it and put into the gas tanks of the consumers.
We are very heavily reliant on imports to provide our source of supply. That is further eroding the value of the dollar. It is further eroding our balance of payments, contributing to high interest rates, destroying confidence in the economy, increasing the outflow of Canadian investment capital, reducing employment opportunities and straining the patience of Canadians. In a letter to the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Lalonde), the Independent Petroleum Association of Canada pointed out the serious difficulties facing the oil production sector in western Canada. Madam Speaker, I would like to quote from this letter which is dated March 5, 1982. It says:
The Independent Petroleum Association of Canada (IPAC) is gravely concerned with the deteriorating market for all Canadian crude oils. Many of our members have been drastically hurt as a result of the loss of production income which seriously affects financing of exploration and production programs.
We all know that the exploration has been reduced by anywhere from 25 per cent to 30 per cent in the year 1981. That is another one of the major job-producing sectors of the petroleum industry. That will be reduced by a further 10 per cent or 15 per cent this year.
It goes on to say:
Many factors impact on the determination of market demand for Canadian crude oil. IPAC is concerned with the effect of the Oil Import Compensation Program, which subsidizes imported crude oil.
For example, our analysis indicates that refiners import foreign heavy crude oil at a net cost of $9. to $12. per barrel less than comparable quality Canadian crudes due to the subsidy.
The inordinately high subsidy paid by Canadian consumers is effectively encouraging crude oil imports, while precluding the production of domestic crude oil. Canadian producers are therefore being forced to shut in their production due to lack of markets. Any subsidy program that encourages foreign crude oil imports, at the expense of Canadian production, requires immediate correction.
Immediate correction, it says. This was dated back on March 5. Over a month has elapsed and nothing has been done. This situation deteriorates further day by day and nothing has been done to correct it. That is absolutely shameful. That is why the Liberal members opposite, who have been asked to vote in support of this measure, should hang their heads in shame.

The second reason why they should hang their heads in shame is over the betrayal of their leader to uphold the election commitment that was taken during the last election campaign.
I have many quotes here, Mr. Speaker, which bear repeating. It really makes a farce out of the whole campaign process. It is little wonder, when the leader of the country was out appealing to Canadians to support him because he was going to keep oil prices down, that he had his followers, who were running for office, doing the same thing; but when they got into office they turned around and really socked it to the consumers.
Look at what the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) said in Toronto on February 8, 1980:
So right from the start, right from the very beginning of a new Liberal government, you will know that the cost of gasoline will not rise by 32 cents a gallon this year. With the 18 cents gone, we will negotiate an oil pricing agreement with the provinces for a price increase of less than $4 a barrel. That would mean less than the 14 cents increase in a gallon of gasoline that the Tories are bringing in this year.
He went on to say in Kamloops, on February 6, 1980:
Liberals would do things differently. First of all, that unfair and unjust 18 cents a gallon gas tax, that 25 cents a gallon diesel tax would not be reimposed. They're unfair, they're unnecessary and they're gone, as far as we are concerned.
Then there were his remarks at Prince Albert, Saskatchewan, on February 5, 1980:
For firsts, we will not reimpose the 18 cents a gallon or the 25 cents a gallon tax. That's inequitable, it's damaging to the economy and as far as we're concerned it's gone. And we will work out with the producing provinces, Alberta, Saskatchewan, British Columbia, a "made in Canada" price for oil and gas and that means a price that will not, as the Tories would have it, that will not automatically be pegged to world prices.
He goes on and on and on. What happened, Mr. Speaker? The fact of the matter is that in that first year there was an increase far in excess of the 14 cents promised. It was more like 28 or 29 cents a gallon. We all know what has happened since then. To date we have had 15 different price increases in the price of gasoline. The tax increases alone in 1981 exceeded more than 32 cents a gallon, almost double the 18 cents that we had proposed. In fact, the latest statistics that I have, show that the national average price of gasoline per gallon in 1979, at the time that this government defeated our government, was $1.14 a gallon; today it is roughly $2 per gallon. Included in that $2 is a provision for a series of taxes which total 60 cents a gallon. That is, 60 cents a gallon of the $2 goes directly into federal government coffers. That is a very good chunk of the total price one pays at the pump.
What is happening, Mr. Speaker, is that in effect, while we have a domestic crude oil price of $23.50, roughly 65 per cent of the world price, we are paying more than the world price at the retail level. What is becoming increasingly disturbing is the fact that while we have prices at the pumps on the increase here in Canada, our counterparts in the United States are finding their prices falling. As a matter of fact, we understand that in the city of Seattle the price of gasoline is roughly 13 cents a gallon lower than what it is in Vancouver.
The Liberal members across should hang their heads in shame because of the betrayal of the election promise. They
Energy Administration Act
have no intention of fulfilling it. This Prime Minister had no intention of doing so, and his major spokesman, his Minister of Finance (Mr. MacEachen), had no intention of fulfilling that election promise. They betrayed the Canadian people with this sleazy tactic. It was sleazy. It has been used as an instrument to divide and to drive a wedge into confederation. I know what they were saying during the last election campaign: "Oh, we are not going to pay that excess tax to build up the coffers of Lougheed's trust fund." That is what they were saying. They were saying: "We cannot afford to make the government of Alberta super rich; we do not mind their getting a fair price, we do not mind their getting rich; but we cannot afford to see them getting super rich."
Well, what they did in the course of their campaign, and what they have done since they formed the government, is divide and further erode the sense of partnership, the sense of togetherness in this country. In effect, they have driven a wedge into confederation. I say to my Liberal friends opposite that they should hang their heads in shame when they are asked to stand and vote in support of this particular measure.
My friend who has just entered the House has been pleading the case for the farmer and I commend him for it. I had a good opportunity of sitting in committee when he challenged the Governor of the Bank of Canada on the high interest rate policy. I know he does it with deep concern and conviction. I would ask him to consider doing something similar to his Minister of Finance and his Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources in respect of the price of diesel fuel-60 cents per gallon in federal tax is being paid by every farmer every time he fills his diesel tractor or combine.
That 60 cents is far too much. There has always been relief for the farmer because he is a producer of food. We have always supported a cheap food policy. We know that the farmers do not have the luxury of passing on these additional costs to the consumer because many of their products are sold on the export market. But 60 cents a gallon is far too much for the farmer to pay in the form of a federal tax. That is another massive revenue grab. For the average farmer in western Canada it means that he has to dig out of his pocket roughly $4,000 to pay into the federal government coffers for that 60 cents a gallon tax that they have imposed upon farm fuel prices. That is grossly unfair. I am sure he would consider it grossly unfair, but I have not heard him say anything about it. It is not the Governor of the Bank of Canada that has imposed this but his own colleagues, the Minister of Finance and the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources.
Let us look at fertilizer, Mr. Speaker. The price of natural gas has a direct impact on the price of fertilizer. They tell me that the federal tax component on production of fertilizer works out anywhere from $25 to $40 a tonne and by 1985 that will increase to about $72 a tonne. That is some 35 per cent of the total cost. That, too, is unfair because the farmer does not have the opportunity of passing that cost on.

We in western Canada also have a grossly unfair pricing structure for fertilizer. The fertilizer manufactured in western Canada and exported to the United States is selling at a price level of between $30 and $60 per tonne less in the United States than it is in Canada. The Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Whelan) said yesterday that that is the free market system working. When he acknowledges that the excessive amount of fertilizer produced in Alberta and Saskatchewan has to be sold in the United States at competitive prices, that simply demonstrates to me that there is not a free marketplace, that the forces of the free market are not working in western Canada because there is either some price fixing or some kind of monopoly. Competitive forces simply are not evident. If they are not evident, surely the minister responsible for farmers and the production of food and the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs (Mr. Ouellet) have a duty and obligation to look into this matter. If this is the market system at work, there is certainly something wrong. In my view, the competitive market system is not at work, and there should be protection for the producers of Canada. We should not tolerate this kind of price gouging.
The farmer is getting it at every end. He is getting it in fertilizer prices, home heating fuel prices and natural gas prices, and he is experiencing an excessive and exorbitant imposition of tax on the diesel fuel he burns in his tractor. That is unfair and it cannot continue.
I hope some hon. members opposite who represent producers as their constituents will think twice before they vote in favour of this particular measure, or at least bring in an amendment which would provide exemptions and some relief for the farmers of Canada. We can bring in amendments. The government will not allow its members to vote with us, but I invite hon. members opposite to do just that. There is no question that we would support them.
This massive rip-off of consumers is something we did not hear much about during the last election campaign. It is no wonder people are losing faith in politicians and the political institutions of this country. When we consider the stupidity of some policies, the blatant deception which occurred during the last election campaign and the lack of confidence in leadership which exists in this country, we see clearly that it is no wonder that there is a sense of hopelessness and despair and a sense that things will get worse before they get better. Canadians are very despondent and frustrated by the fact that there is no hope on the horizon because of the silly and asinine policies which are in effect. We are not asking for anything dramatic. We are asking for nothing in the way of favouritism. We are just asking for a little commonsense.
We are debating here a Canadian ownership charge, and that brings me to Petro-Canada. Petro-Canada was something which was urgently needed to provide oil self-sufficiency to the country. The creature was created at a cost of some $4 billion. Today we are more reliant on imported oil than we were a year ago, and a year ago we were more reliant on imported oil than the year before.
What has Petro-Canada done? It has taken over going concerns at very heavy cost to the people of Canada. Petro-Canada is involved in places like Tanzania, Senegal, Kenya, Jamaica, Bangladesh, Pakistan and many other countries of the world, but we do not see Petro-Canada doing any pioneering or trail-blazing here in Canada. Petro-Canada has done nothing to improve our level of self-sufficiency. It puts out nice ads. Petro-Canada can hire American advertising consultants to define its trademarks, and so forth but Petro-Canada has become a joke.
No one really expects Petro-Canada to wave a magic wand and provide us with energy self-sufficiency. Petro-Canada has hired a number of bureaucrats and more government appointments have been made. Petro-Canada has become another reward centre for the diminishing number of people who have some sympathy for the Liberal cause. The whole philosophy and attitude of the government is that it should corral revenue so that the government can impose central control, assert authority, determine where growth will take place and in what region, how resources are to be developed, who will get the nod to do such development and who the winners and losers will be. The price we are paying for that kind of philosophy is seen in the growing numbers of people on unemployment rolls, the growing numbers of people who are losing their homes and the growing numbers of businesses closing their doors. Farm bankruptcies are up 50 per cent this year over last year. What is happening is that while the productive labour force is being reduced, the non-productive government labour force is being increased. The March 22 editorial of The Financial Times points that out:
But the policies of the Trudeau government in this recession are having a curious effect: the producers are losing their jobs and the non-producers are cruising through unscathed.
The layoffs announced week-by-week by hard-hit companies are almost all among producers. There are 133,000 fewer manufacturing jobs in Canada than there were a year ago, according to Statistics Canada. Jobs in primary industry have dropped by 41,000. Construction jobs are down 17,000.
On the other hand, the category of "public administration" had 770,000 jobs in February, 26,000 more than four months earlier on a seasonally-adjusted basis.
The article goes on:
A year ago the federal staff numbered about 329,000. Ottawa expects this to grow to 334,000 by the end of this month. And the government is planning to have 345,000 employees by a year from now. To be comparable, these totals include postal workers.
Not only does the number of bureaucrats grow throughout recessions but it continues to grow in times-such as the present-when the government proclaims that it is following a policy of restraint.
In the past year, for instance, the federal energy department has added 656 new employees, a 17 per cent increase. And that doesn't count the 1,639 employees added by Petro-Canada.
What are companies in the private sector doing? They have to lay people off. Because of the decline in the petroleum industry, a reduction in the work force is necessary. We have a paradox. The government payroll is exploding, and the private sector-the productive sector-payroll is on the decline. Oil companies are being squeezed by falling demand and rising taxes, while at the same time there is an explosion of jobs in

the non-productive government sector. That is essentially what is happening in this country.
As I said in a speech earlier this week, the productive labour force in Canada is reducing. Production in this country is reducing. We have not had any new wealth generated over the last five years, and unless we start generating some new wealth, unless we start encouraging production and productivity and unless we can experience some real growth in this country, we will be in very, very serious trouble. We cannot continue to redistribute wealth. We have to create and generate some new wealth, and that is something this government is not doing.
I want to turn now to what I consider another classic example of stupidity and discrimination, and it has to do with the treatment of fuel tax with respect to Canadian air carriers. We are all aware that there has been a transportation fuel compensation recovery charge levied against our airlines and our ships which are involved in export trade. This primarily affects the ships employed in the coastal trade and service on the Great Lakes. We know that some $50 million in taxes has been imposed on internationally schedule and charter services. Because the tax is discriminatory and has violated bilateral agreements made with other countries, the government decided to rebate some $46 million of export fuel taxes to the foreign carriers that serve Canada but it has refused to treat Canadian carriers in the same way. There is a double standard, Mr. Speaker, and it just does not make sense. The decision places Canadian carriers at a severe financial disadvantage relative to foreign competitors. This threatens the financial health of Canadian airlines at a time of seriously depressed earnings.
This case has a long history, Mr. Speaker. The Air Transport Association of Canada warned the government at the time that this action would be in clear violation of the bilateral agreements. Foreign governments made representations to the Canadian authorities and they finally agreed to the exemption. But it has not been provided to Canadian carriers, Mr. Speaker, so again there is a double standard which works to Canadians' disadvantage.
This bill proposes that a tax of approximately eight cents per litre or 36 cents per gallon be imposed upon the supplier-a sort of income tax on refiners and/or suppliers. It blatantly interferes with contract negotiations between airlines and their suppliers.
Until now, fuel products exported in the east were levied a charge to recover compensation on the originally imported oil. This charge will extend this treatment to the west and will impose it on all Canadian aircraft leaving Canada. There is no reference to the level of the charge to be levied. The export charge on diesel type fuels, called middle distillates, was about $113 per cubic meter while the fuel compensation recovery charge for February was only in the $47 to $68 range. There are differences in the recovery charge for the type of user and point of departure. The charge on the east coast for marine
Energy Administration Act
diesel is $78.35 while the charge for the west coast is $47.20 for February.
We have to ask why the bill does not mention that different classes of users will be charged different amounts. The bill should speak to this and the minister should explain the difference between the two costs.
The bill does not speak to the adjustments that have been made to the charge with respect to airlines. The government has indicated that this charge will no longer be levied on aircraft and that they will use the income tax system to capture back the same amount as the charge, yet the bill is silent on this point. A charge of nil for February is insufficient to guarantee that the charge will never be levied again.
There is confusion and discrimination in this, Mr. Speaker. The airlines are not arguing about the fact that the taxes are to be imposed but about the method in which they are being imposed. They believe that this constitutes a gross interference in contract negotiations between the airlines and the suppliers of fuel. This demonstrates again the effects that a myriad of regulations, excessive costs, a variety of taxes, levies and surcharges will have and they have to be coped with in the consideration of this legislation. It is a bureaucrat's and accountant's haven but it is a burden to anyone who wants to live up to the spirit and letter of the law.
We are in the final throes of debating a program which, as I said the other day, will go down in history as the major manmade disaster of the 1980s-the National Energy Program. This series of bills should be considered with a great deal of caution and care and there should be the greatest input possible from the people who will be affected by them, directly or indirectly, and that is the people in the industry. I refer not only to the multinationals and the big oil companies but to the average individual and the average company that is part and parcel of this network that is the petroleum industry in Canada.
This has become a very important and viable industry, Mr. Speaker. While my province and western Canada have an agricultural based economy, in places like Vegreville, Lloyd-minister, Wainwright, Vermilion, Cold Lake, Leduc, Wetaski-win, the oil industry, in various forms, is a very important component of the health of the whole economy. It provides an economic spin-off, a tax base and an economic development base. We need all of these in western Canada to provide some security so that our economy will not be dependent on one industry or another.
That component of our economy has been hurt very badly. People who have invested their lifetime earnings in aspects of the oil service, drilling and exploration industry have been hurt very badly. Companies that have been in existence for 10 or 20 years have been forced to lay-off large numbers of people. In some cases they have been forced to close their doors. All this because of a man-made, deliberate policy which is seen as an attack on the west and an attack upon industry.
The agricultural industry and the oil industry have worked hand in hand, Mr. Speaker. Of course, there have been times

It summarizes, in layman's language, the serious and combined impact of the budgets of 1980, 1981 and the National Energy Program. Under the heading "Let's do Something" it reads as follows:
It has been a relatively short time since the Budget and National Energy Program were delivered to the Canadian people. In this time, residents of Canada have gone from the inquisitive to the unbelieving.
In the short span of 16 months, many businesses have gone under-the victims of high interest rates. Many farms and ranches have followed suit.
Today, people meeting on the street no longer follow the customary greeting whith a smile. Now they ask each other how they are surviving.
We have watched helplessly as businesses closed their doors and silently disappeared. We have listened on the phone while well-respected business people tell us they just don't have the funds to pay an account. We have heard about the countless hardships a farmer has mastered throughout his life-until now.
We have watched while our country's once strong economic situation turned for the worse.
