Mr. Speaker, we have just heard from the hon. member for Vegreville (Mr. Mazankowski) a moving and masterful exposition of the depth of the dangers our country faces. I congratulate him on that speech and, sir, as I speak in the same vein as the hon. member, I hope you will interpret my remarks as coming out of the depth of the west. For indeed, Sir, virtually every member of this House from western Canada feels the same as myself, the hon. member for Vegreville and the others who have spoken in this debate.
In the light of statistical indicators, Mr. Speaker, it is evident the federal government's record on economic affairs is abysmal. But on energy matters the record is horrendous. Energy policies have been constructed out of political expend-iency or gross misreading of the economy and the country's total needs. It was political expediency which led the government to embark on the ill-advised policy of shielding the Canadian consumer from the effects of OPEC price increases in 1973. It gave the consumer the illusion that he lived in the best of all possible worlds. The Canadian consumer did not learn to conserve, industry was not helped to adjust to the new reality, and the government did not push for self-sufficiency with the force it should have. Now, finally, the consumer is painfully waking up, and industry has to make adjustments in often tragic ways.
On energy matters, of which this bill is a prime example, the government is still acting in a woefully erroneous fashion. Let me put it plainly: the national energy policy is an unmitigated disaster, not just for my province, but for the whole country.
As a Canadian I am truly saddened to see what is happening in my country; not only the loss of jobs, but the fear which is sweeping across the land. Millions of Canadians today fear for their continued employment. What is worse, as the Gallup poll has just shown, a large section of the public fears that if they do lose their jobs, they will not be able to get another one. What kind of society is that?
As an Albertan I am angered at the loss of potential. The national energy policy ignores the needs and aspirations of all Canadians and has its deepest negative effects on Alberta. Of course, Mr. Speaker, I stand for Canadianization, greater control of the industry in Canadian hands. As the Conservative party finance critic, the hon. member for Etobicoke Centre (Mr. Wilson), stated publicly on July 21, 1981, "this is an economic fact of life and the reversal of a process which has occurred in Canada over the past 100 years".
But, sir, Canadianization should not be confused with nationalization. Yet that is what the government is doing. It is softening up the stock market and buying into the industry at depressed price levels. Surely it is open for all to see how oil share prices declined when the NEP was announced. Virtually the only major stock which did not lose was Petrofina, which the government later purchased at a grossly inflated price. Yes, Canadianization should be our goal, but not through nationalization or the strategy this government is following. "Canadian owned" does not and ought not mean "Canadian government owned". The Canadian private sector ought to be encouraged to invest in the energy industry.
This, Mr. Speaker, is why the Progressive Conservative Party in 1979 proposed the Canadian common stock investment plan. Canadians investing in Canada was the object of that plan. Small investors were to be encouraged to participate in Canadian-owned companies. RRSPs were to be encouraged to purchase Canadian stocks. We were even planning, as is well known, to offer shares in Petro-Canada to Canadians at $10 a share, not the $120 which the government is asking for shares in a PetroCan subsidiary. The present government has not even looked at this kind of measure. Instead by imposing a 25 per cent retroactive back-in on federal lands, it has made prospective investors ask: Will our money be safe there?
It is this lack of investor confidence, this basic uncertainty about the Canadian government's intentions, which is causing many firms to sell out and others to move to the United States. Small Canadian firms would rather be involved here in Canada if conditions permitted them to be, but they go to the United States because their policies make energy investment increasingly attractive. We now find that 12 per cent of the oil and natural gas exploration in the United States is being undertaken by Canadian companies, and that is why I, as an Albertan, am angry. Most of the companies which have moved to the United States have moved from Alberta. Two hundred and thirty-one oil drilling rigs have lefts since the NEP was announced, along with 111 service rigs. That is as if in Ontario or Quebec small factories employing 40 or 50 had closed down one by one. Drilling activity in 1981 was up 26 per cent over

1980 in the United States, and it was down by the same amount in Canada.

speechtext:
It is my duty, pursuant to Standing Order 40, to inform the House that the questions to be raised tonight at the time of adjournment are as follows: the hon. member for La Prairie (Mr. Deniger)-Airports-Future of Dorval and Mirabel; the hon. member for Winnipeg North (Mr. Orlikow)-Bankruptcies-(a) Increase in number-(b) Request that government take action; the hon. member for Brant (Mr. Blackburn)-Foreign Investment Review Agency-(a) Takeover of White Farm Equipment Company by Texas firm, (b) Patents for Canadian-produced combine, (c) Possibility of Canadian control.

It being five o'clock, the House will now proceed to the consideration of private members' business as listed on today's Order Paper, namely, notices of motions (papers).
[DOT] (UOO)

That an Order of the House do issue for copies of all questionnaires given to public servants and all studies made by the Treasury Board in 1980 and 1981 in connection with day care centres.
He said: First, I would like to thank the seconder of the motion for enabling me to speak on it. He is not aware of my remarks and has not expressed any approval of what I am going to say, and for that matter he has not expressed any opinion. He has simply, by seconding the motion, given me the opportunity to speak.
I want to make it quite clear that the subject is not day care centres. I want to say, as I have said in this House previously, that the issue is administration, control, government spending, government procedures and for that matter even House procedures. These are the topics I will be discussing this afternoon.
Day Care Centres
Before departing from the words "day care centre", let me reiterate what I have said previously in this House. I want to see a system of day care centres throughout the public service.
I want to see them efficiently operated and I want to see a subsidy program provided, either at the provincial or federal level or at both levels of government so that these day care centres will be accessible to all children of public servants and not just to those whose parents have large enough incomes to afford to pay what I consider to be very high cost.
Putting that aside, let us look at what I consider is the issue I want to discuss this afternoon. Why, as a start, did I transfer motion No. 86 for debate and not allow any further time for the production of the documents asked for in the motion? Simply because I have put several notices on the Order Paper. Notice of motion No. 85 and this one called for documents from the Department of Public Works in connection with the construction program in the last fiscal year ending March 31, 1982.
On February 24, the motion was agreed to. I thought I would be receiving the required documents. I was completely amazed at what was handed to me. I received two sheets of paper which were generalities and were, in effect, a reiteration of what started this exercise, namely a news release dated June 26, 1981. In fact, attached to those two sheets of paper was the news release of June 26, 1981. That was the answer to the motion. That was the answer to what I consider was the order of the House to produce estimates and plans for the day care centre so we could see ourselves what costs were envisaged and what plans were being made.
I brought up this matter in the House and discussed it. The Speaker, and I do not take issue with the ruling, said there was nothing she could do. However, what it does for me is clearly illustrate that a motion passed by this House which becomes an order of the House is valueless. Nothing is produced. Nothing need be produced and there is no means by which a member can ensure the production of documents.
I was particularly annoyed because I had seen certain of the documents. As a result of my comments made in the House and as a result of some pressure I brought to bear on the Minister of Public Works (Mr. Cosgrove), the plans which I had already seen and which I assume are the only plans were produced for me. I was able to review them. They are very extensive. They are very well put together. Along with them I received what purports to be a fairly extensive specification.
I now know why these documents were not tabled. It is because they are in one language only, the English language. I suggest that we have gone past the stage where documents for use on the Hill should be in only one of our official languages. I asked myself how any workman who just happens to be unilingual French is able to understand either the plans or the specifications. But apart from that, I have still not seen any estimates. Being a construction man, I am aware that when one attends to demolition, to all kinds of renovation work, moves libraries, messenger services, does landscaping and
16510

April 22, 1982
Day Care Centres
builds fences, some fairly detailed estimates ordinarily should be prepared. What we were given was a global figure.
I eventually got this information in a letter from the Minister of Public Works. The subject of the letter is the day care centre. The issue is not the day care centre itself; it is the way we handle costs. The cost shown for the architectural, mechanical, electrical, structural and outside play areas is $210,000. That is a nice global figure. Next we find fees and miscellaneous costs including management and contingency sums, for another $30,000. That totals $240,000. That figure was produced in a committee hearing as being the cost to public works of doing this work in one of our buildings on the Hill.
Being always somewhat cautious when figures are bandied around in such global fashion, I enquired and found out that there is another cost involved namely the cost of related work including the relocation of the branch library-we would not have had to relocate the branch library if we had not been building the day care centre-the messenger service and the traffic control services, which will be in the order of $80,000. When we are spending $80 billion, I suppose $80,000 is relatively insignificant, but it bothers me. It bothers me because as far as I am concerned when we spend money here it is coming out of my pocket in the form of taxes and I want to see better control.
But that is not the end. We now have $240,000 plus $80,000 which equals $320,000. Loose equipment and furniture will be purchased separately. I do not know how much that will be, I have no idea. But we are now looking at an expenditure in the order of $400,000 for 40 children, or $10,000 per head.
I love children, Mr. Speaker. I want every child in this country to have the opportunity my two children had of going to a day care centre and receiving that kind of advanced training before attending primary school. But to tell me, a construction man, that we have to spend $10,000 per head for every child going to a day care centre is, I suggest, absolutely ludicrous. 1 object and I object very strongly.
What is worse is found in a letter from the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Miss Begin) who writes:
According to what I have been told, the day care centre in the Confederation Building will be run by a board of directors independent of the House of Commons administration.
That is probably a good thing. The Minister's letter continues:
-moderate-income employees, earning $15,000 or $20,000 a year, are far less able to pay the day care fees than a higher-income person.
That is absolutely correct, particularly when one finds that person is ordinarily a single family parent with two children. The cost to that person will be $650 a month for 12 months. We should look at the total. It is absolutely beyond the reach of most employees on the Hill. The minister went on to say:
I have therefore asked my officials if employees using the Confederation Building day care centre (and similar centres at other places of employment)-
We must remember that this is an example for the country. This is what we will hopefully be able to do throughout the public service as an employer. She continued:
-might be eligible for subsidies but would be cost-shared under the Canada Assistance Plan.
Then a memo in this connection was attached, and she went on to say:
As you will see, it is possible for CAP cost-sharing to be available for children enrolled in the centre. However, most federal employees would probably not be eligible for subsidies because their incomes would exceed the levels that have been set by the province of Ontario.
Essentially day care centres are in the provincial sphere of jurisdiction. The province is responsible for the control, the province decides the level to which they will be subsidized, and the province in that regard also sets the amount of participation of the federal government because the federal government pays 50 per cent of whatever the province decides to pay.
To ascertain exactly what kind of organization would be running the centre, I put questions. First I should explain once again that it is not because this is a day care centre which we pass every day; I am looking at examples of the way we operate and the money we spend for what we will be doing in the entire public service. I want it kept in that perspective. If we are to establish boards for every day care centre in different departments of government, apparently this is the manner in which they will be set up, through independent boards. I asked how the board was selected, who decided on the membership, and why there were no men on the board.
We have been fighting so-called discrimination. Normally when we think of discrimination, it is in the terms that women are not considered equal. I object as a male from being excluded from the consideration of what will happen to my children or the children of other people. I have every right to do so. I was not given an answer. In fact, the response was simple: "Ask the board." I asked the board who selected it and why its members were all women. Frankly, I think the whole matter is becoming somewhat ludicrous.
What was the answer?
I did not obtain an answer, because obtaining an answer here is sometimes a very lengthy process.
We know that better than you.

I am called upon to speak in the House long before the answer finally comes to me.
This centre, which will be the example in the public service, will be entirely self-supporting. How can we say that it will be entirely self-supporting when the cost is $10,000 per child at the outset? The interest on those moneys alone is at least $1,500 per annum per child. There are public funds involved, and since they will not be recovered, it is not self-supporting at the onset. Therefore, as government policy, why do we not accept that we will be involved in a considerable expenditure of funds and say, in all fairness to the population, that we should add the required subsidies to ensure that the facilities are available to everyone on an equal basis? How can we expect
April 22, 1982

any of the ladies who work in our cafeterias, or even the men who drive our buses, to have the necessary funds to put their children into this very expensive, very nice, very attractive and very laudable day care centre? They will not have access to it, and on that basis I think it is something at which the government must look. I feel it is discriminatory.
I have raised several points this afternoon. Before we go any further, we must look at our total approach. The memorandum or the communique issued on June 26 should be followed up with a reasonably good study of exactly what we are getting into. Having identified what initial costs are involved, we should look at what additional costs will have to be added to construction costs in order to make the centre accessible to all employees. Furthermore, there should be a little more consultation with the province of Ontario. The centre is to be licensed by the day nurseries branch of the Ontario Department of Social and Family Services. This is fine. I suppose it means that they will be responsible for the general overhaul of its facilities to ensure that they are suitable and presumably ensure that it is run according to good standards. I think I have made my point. We have spent a lot of money and we are continuing to do so.
In conclusion, I should like to refer to one item which bothers me somewhat. The procedures by which we operate on a fiscal basis whereby everything ends on March 31, I find irritating. I have discussed, for example, control of costs with the Auditor General. It will be realized that any construction which goes over a year's end finds costs in two different fiscal years. Under those circumstances it is very difficult to put together a package. We must add to that the fact that moneys are coming out of three completely different pockets-one for the construction, one for the moving of library, messenger services and so on, and one for the supply of furniture and various fixtures. One can see that it will probably be at least the autum of 1983 before we as Members of Parliament will see the dollars involved. I do not consider that a very satisfactory procedure. I plead with the President of the Treasury Board (Mr. Johnston) to put the cards on the table, to tell us precisely what is involved and to tell us precisely what is his intention. He should assure us that it is government policy, if it is going into the field of day care centres, to ensure that day care facilities are available to all public service employees regardless of their levels of income.

Mr. Speaker, 1 commend the hon. member for Vaudreuil (Mr. Herbert) for his concern about accessibility to the day care centre being constructed on the Hill. If I understand correctly, at this point there will be no subsidized spaces in the day care centre, but there is some hope that there might be some in the future.
This is an excellent opportunity to impress upon not only one government member, the hon. member for Vaudreuil, but upon all government members who are present, the need for a national day care act. In this case, if there was an appropriate act, it would provide guidelines for the provision of subsidized spaces in this day care centre as in all other day care centres
Day Care Centres
which exist or come into existence, whether they be in the public service or anywhere else.
Today I would like to take the opportunity to put some facts on the record with regard to day care in Canada and to make some suggestions from the New Democratic Party point of view. In this regard, I would like to refer generally to the analysis of day care in Canada which is found in the annual health and welfare publication, "Status of Day Care in Canada." I would refer particularly to the one which was recently released which has some interesting statistics.
The amount of licensed or supervised day care space increased in 1980 by 16.8 per cent. Non-commercial space increased by 33 per cent and commercial space decreased by
3.7	per cent. This was the reverse from the year before when the growth in space was concentrated in the "day care for profit" sector.
Infant day care centres continue to be the big loser. It is estimated that in 1980 there were 229,000 children under the age of two whose mothers were in the labour force. A total of
3.8	per cent of these children are receiving group care or approved family day care service. As of March, 1980 there were an estimated 531,000 children aged two to six of working mothers. The data indicates that that 15.77 per cent of these children are enrolled in day care services. The conglomerate figures show that of the 760,000 children under the age of six whose mothers are in the work force, only 12.6 per cent of them are in approved day care spaces. This was a marginal improvement over the previous year's figures of 12.04 per cent. The fact remains that fully 88 per cent of Canada's children under the age of six whose mothers are in the labour force are left in unlicensed child care arrangements.
A further breakdown of day care centre spaces reveals that the overwhelming percentage of day care spaces are being utilized by children between the ages of two and six, some 79.94 per cent. Spaces for children under the age of two represent 5.38 per cent of all centre spaces, which is down by 400 spaces from 1979. This represents an acute problem for parents with infants.
Our short-term, low-benefit maternity benefits make day care that much more essential. We passed a resolution at our federal convention in 1979 calling for an increased federal share of cost sharing for infant day care spaces as a mechanism for increasing accessibility to this very important kind of care.
I will now give a few provincial comparisons, for those who may be interested. As indicated in this study, each province has its own mix of day care delivery, as we might expect. Ontario and Alberta are the only two provinces which have publicly owned-that is to say, municipally owned-day care centres. The municipalities in both of these provinces have had an active involvement in the delivery of day care services and, in both provinces, contribute to the cost of day care.

April 22, 1982
Day Care Centres
Non-profit day care centres are predominant in British Columbia, Saskatchewan, Manitoba and Quebec. In Saskatchewan, only parent co-operatives qualify for licensing. In Ontario, commercial and non-profit centres are approximately equal in numbers. Commercial centres in Alberta outnumber non-profit centres by two to one. In five of ten provinces, that is Ontario, New Brunswick, Alberta, Newfoundland and Prince Edward Island, one half or more of the spaces are commercial, principally serving the needs of full fee-paying parents.
As I have mentioned, in light of the great need which remains to be met in terms of providing day care services in Canada, we have passed a number of resolutions in our party having to do with this concern. I would like to indicate one resolution for the record which was passed at the federal convention of 1979 which continues to be New Democratic Party policy:
THEREFORE BE IT RESOLVED that the NDP reaffirm its 1971 commitment that an NDP Federal Government would enact a national Child Care Act; commit itself to the philosophy of child care as a public service, and initiate an educational campaign in support of this philosophy.
BE IT FURTHER RESOLVED that in the meantime, as a matter of urgency, the NDP press for:
(1)	initiatives on the part of the Federal Government by offering preferential cost-sharing schemes (ie. paying 75 per cent of the capital cost of building child care centres, 80 per cent of the cost of child care staff, increasing the federal part of cost-sharing child care services for infants and handicapped children) thereby increasing the accessibility and quality of childcare;
(2)	the encouragement of provincial and municipal governments to make child care a higher budgetary priority and to institute a ceiling on child care fees charged to parents;
The fourth point in this resolution stated:
(4) legislation be passed requiring employers to fund quality day care centres in the workplace.
Policy resolutions are always an indication of rough intention. I believe that these policies which were passed by the national convention of the NDP are worthy of consideration.
I would like to dwell for a minute on a matter which concerns me, not just with respect to day care but to nursing homes and anything having to do with the provision of human services, for that matter. It concerns the ongoing debate about whether or not such services can be provided adequately within the context of profit-making institutions. While we have always had profit-oriented day care centres, we see more of them coming into being, especially now since we see multinational day care corporations such as Kindercare moving into this field. They obviously see it as an area in which they might be able to make money.
I would like to reflect for a moment on some of the drawbacks to profit-oriented day care. First, since fees are limited by what parents can afford to pay, making a profit from day care necessitates cutting back on the quality of day care provided. Another point is that the issue of quality of care is primary given the argument that good quality care cannot be provided on a profit-making basis. For instance, a recent investigation into the expenditures of profit-oriented day care centres in the United States concluded that:
For-profit centres typically spend much less per child than do non-profit centres. According to the 1977 Abt. data, average annual expenditures per child are about 30 per cent lower in for-profit centres than in non-profit centres.
Most of these expenditure savings are made through lower staff salaries. Lower salaries tend to mean less trained and less experienced staff and a higher turnover which disrupts relationships within the day care centre.
A 1979 Toronto survey of 30 for-profit and 91 non-profit centres found that staff salaries were significantly lower in for-profit centres. This same survey found that for-profit oriented centres provided fewer staff benefits, including paid vacation, sick leave, pension plans, life insurance and in the case of Ontario, OHIP payments. In Edmonton, a survey by health inspectors reported that almost half the for-profit centres were not providing adequate care. In Ottawa, purchase of service agreements has just been withdrawn from two profit oriented centres due to misuse of funds.
A further criticism of for-profit centres is that they do not encourage or, in some cases, even permit parental involvement. The special nature of day care in providing care for very young children makes the involvement of parents in the substitute care particularly desirable. Apart from the lack of parental involvement and questionable quality of present centres, the continued growth of for-profit day care, particularly corporate centres, as I have mentioned, raises the possibility of future lobbying activity to lower standards in day care.
I want to say that even though I have outlined many of the inadequacies which arise as a result of operating day care centres according to the profit motive, I would still have some concern even if it could be demonstrated to me that profit-oriented day care centres do provide good quality care from time to time. I am concerned about the long-range trend which is particularly in evidence in the United States, but I am also concerned that it might become a trend here to perceive human services as a new and challenging field for the marketplace. I am concerned that we will see more and more of this as traditional sources of capital and profit move into the Third World, as we try to export pollution and some of the more negative consequences of industrial society, and that here in North America we will see a move toward more commercialization of human services. We will see this through multinational corporations involved in nursing home care and in the provision of day care, and in the provision of health services, so that finally no area of human activity will be left untouched by this particular manner of regard for human life and all things will be turned into commodities in the marketplace.
It would be a mistake to see my concern about profit-oriented day care as part and parcel of the old and sometimes boring debate between those who would like to see something done by the private sector and those who would like to see something done by the public sector. As I mentioned in the energy debate just a few days ago, our debates in this country must transcend those two caricatures, because I am not interested in a broad, monolithic, all-pervasive multinational human service industry. But, neither am I interested in a broad, monolithic, all-pervasive, government-run bureaucratic human service industry either. What we should advocate in
April 22, 1982

this country is that all day care centres be run as far as possible on a parent involved basis, a community involved basis. We should look to smaller scale, more co-operative, community based enterprises, particularly when we are concerned with something as important as child care. So that is what I have in mind. We need to transcend the debate over which bureaucracy is to run our lives, whether public bureaucracy or private bureaucracy, as it is a sort of rut that we tend to get into here due to certain, long-standing ideological battles.
That is about all I have to say on this matter. I did not want to get into the details of what the hon. member for Vaudreuil (Mr. Elerbert) said concerning the day care centre which is now on the Hill; I will leave that for another day. However, 1 wanted to take this opportunity to put on the record our concern that no leadership is being shown by the federal government in the matter of ensuring adequate child care services for Canadians right across the country. We think the federal government ought to show some leadership in the way it previously did with regard to health care and other human services. This should be done, particularly in light of today's economic conditions when many women must go out to work, whether they like it or not.
A number of factors are involved, including the economic factor. Many times both parents must go out to work simply to make ends meet, not simply because there is any particular moment of liberation. Perhaps there is also the factor of changes taking place in the perception of the role of women in our society. Both of these factors are combining to create the need for more options when it comes to child care.
Those who lament the passing of the traditional perception of the family ought simultaneously to lament the fact that the particular economic system in which we live has brought us to the point where couples cannot afford to have one or the other spouse, whether it be the man or the woman, staying home to provide child care. When we say that the need for day care is compulsory rather than voluntary, 1 think that although this need is to be regretted, it is necessary. To the extent that it opens up opportunities for women in particular and for married couples in general to pursue different employment alternatives and other courses of action in their lives, 1 think the provision of day care is a good thing and the need ought to be met on that basis as well.
I rise on a point of order, Mr. Speaker. In view of the fact that the time allotted to the hon. member has not expired, I wonder whether he would accept a question from me.
Surely.

speechtext: Is that agreed? It is agreed.

Mr. Speaker, in view of the fact that it is generally accepted that this type of care for children is within the provincial sphere of influence and that federal intervention is either financial, through the Canada Assistance Plan, or, in the present case, as an employer, has the New Democratic
Day Care Centres
Party looked at the jurisdictional problem, particularly considering the fact that there is a variation of treatment from province to province and that all children across this country do not have access to similar centres because of the difference in provincial treatment? Has the New Democratic Party considered the jurisdictional problem and has it come up with any recommendations?

Mr. Speaker, by virtue of our intention to have a national child care act, we have indicated it is possible this is an area in which there might be joint federal-provincial responsibility; indeed, there already is joint responsibility. As the hon. member for Vaudreuil mentioned once before, certain day care spaces are already under federal responsibility in so far as they are cost-shared under the Canada Assistance Plan. The problem of the federal government concerning that particular type of day care is that it is only available to people who meet the criterion for assistance under the Canada Assistance Plan of being in need or likely to be in need.
What we are saying is that all day care ought to be seen as a necessary social service rather than a welfare or handout provision for certain families. In many cases, the people who now qualify for social assistance or who meet the criterion set by the provinces to show that they are in need or likely to be in need qualify for day care. Of course, people with a lot of money qualify for day care because they can pay for it; but the people in the middle are the ones who really find it difficult and must make difficult decisions as to whether or not they can recover enough money from their jobs to have some left over after they have paid for day care. However, if the federal government provided some leadership and some money, I do not think it would have much difficulty with the provinces in trying to provide some leadership in that area.

Mr. Speaker, let me say that I am very pleased to be able to speak for just a few moments in this debate on the motion of the hon. member for Vaudreuil (Mr. Herbert), who has a habit of bringing some very interesting motions to the House of Commons. It is interesting that he, being a Liberal, is always bringing motions that an order of the House issue for copies of all questionnaires given to public servants and all studies made by Treasury Board in 1981 in connection with day care centres and other matters. I would have thought as a Liberal he could just open his mouth quietly in caucus and the documentation would flow out. I thought these denial of information requests were something endemic to our side of the House. I now find that the caucus system we hear about is not as open as it should be.
My friend used a phrase in the course of his interesting speech that was important. I followed his speech and, I must say, generally approved. I think I can quote him correctly. He said it was time the President of the Treasury Board (Mr. Johnston) came clean and told us exactly what is going on. That is true.

April 22, 1982
Day Care Centres
As I go about my constituency and this general area, in this era when women are trying to break out of occupations heretofore reserved to women, trying to exercise professional talents that have been gained because they have ventured educationally and are prepared to venture otherwise into areas heretofore occupied by men or believed to be the domain of men, I am amazed at the tremendous interest in the provision of day care.
Day care serves two social obligations that are mixed and are not really in conflict. First, there is an obligation to recognize the importance of providing every opportunity to equalize opportunities to the greatest possible degree with regard to participation in the work force. Second, the caring and rearing of children, although it is a primary obligation of the family, is not just an obligation of the family but an obligation of society as well. As society evolves, so must our institutions.
I have not seen copies of the documents and questionnaires which my friend has asked for. I am interested in seeing them. The essence of his motion and the questions he asks is that when dealing with day care in terms of the public service, it must be dealt with on a fair, reasonable and universal basis. There cannot be one system, whether it is here in the House of Commons or anywhere else in the public service, for the well-to-do, or no system or a different system for those who are not so well-to-do. That is the matter which concerns me.
Opportunities for work ought to be equal regardless of the economic status of the person whose family requires day care. They ought to be open in a systemic sense to all of those who require day care.
I congratulate the hon. member for Vaudreuil (Mr. Herbert). I have done this on other occasions. I join him in his request for information with respect to this matter. It is important. Every time one goes around one's constituency, one finds how important this question and issue is, and the solutions we seek.
I repeat, there is a mixed obligation toward the maintenance, rearing and care of children. Although it is primary, it is just not the obligation of the family. The community has an obligation to ensure that in a changing world children are granted proper care. Opportunities must be given to those who without those facilities would not be able to advance equally with others.
I commend my hon. friend. I will not take any more time of the House. 1 hope that someone on the government side will stand up and say to the hon. member for Vaudreuil, "Here are your documents"; and when he gets them, that he will share them with me.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the President of the Treasury Board
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is a privilege to speak this afternoon in the "Hal Herbert hour". 1 will preface my remarks by pointing out to the hon. member for Nepean-Carleton (Mr. Baker) and the hon. member for Vaudreuil (Mr. Herbert) that no studies have been produced or made public, for the simple reason that no studies were done in 1980, 1981, before or after, by Treasury Board. The absence of these studies should not reflect badly on the department nor on the
way in which our fabled caucus works internally behind closed doors.
I wish to divide my remarks this afternoon into three sections. First, in a very general way I will deal with women in the workplace and the relationship of this government to them. Second, I will deal in a general way with day care centres and the reasons for them. Third, I will deal with the experience of this government in handling day care within the jurisdiction of the federal government.
Females in the workplace is a topic that all of us in this House take seriously. We do so because not only are females a large percentage of today's work force, but every study I have ever read indicates they will become an increasingly larger component of the work force in the years that lie ahead. Unfortunately, there are a number of forces that historically and physiologically work against full and complete participation by females in the work force.
The cultural disadvantage that I am alluding to is that traditionally we have reserved the best or highest paying jobs for males. We tend in our promoting practices, consciously or unconsciously, to choose male applicants over female applicants. Physiologically, a woman is disadvantaged, or at least her working life is complicated, by the fact that quite often she has to bear the simultaneous dual role of worker and mother. I wish to state for the record this afternoon that this government and this party is committed to fighting the first cultural disadvantage and to help women reach a satisfactory accommodation of the second disadvantage.
This is a Liberal government, this is a Liberal Party and the essence of Liberalism is to liberate. I would like everyone in this House to know that this government is dedicated to liberation of women in the workplace, whether it be the federal workplace in Ottawa or other federal workplaces across Canada, or in the marketplace in general.
There is evidence of that statement, Mr. Speaker. There is the creation of the Royal Commission on the Status of Women, the creation of the Office of Equal Opportunities which was established in 1971, the announcement by Treasury Board in 1975 of a policy to promote a greater representation of females in the federal work force.
Furthermore, I would bring your attention to the publication of a plan of action in 1979 and to the pronouncement by the President of the Treasury Board (Mr. Johnston) in June, 1981, of the day care policy-to which the hon. member from Vaudreuil alluded earlier in his speech. I would hope that there is no one in this House who would believe that day care is a luxury. All too often when talking privately in a party or a gathering of some sort, we hear people complain about the cost of day care, as if day care were a luxury that we could not afford.
I would argue that day care, far from being a luxury, is indeed a necessity, not only a social necessity but an economic
April 22, 1982

necessity. That latter statement, that day care is an economic necessity, is a point that needs to be stressed this afternoon and at any time when a debate arises over the need for day care centres.
For example, an employer-or a body like an employer, such as this government is-should recognize that the creation of day care centres on site, in the workplace, has significant economic advantages to that company. For example, day care centres certainly attract employees. A company's ability to get good employees is enhanced if the prospective employees know and understand that there will be facilities at the work site for their children. Day care centres already in operation in the work force prove conclusively that they lead to lower absten-teeism.
Absenteeism today is a growing problem in the work force. I have talked to businessmen in my riding about their labour situation. One of the criticisms that I hear most often is that it is hard to get good employees. Secondly, it is hard to keep them working on the job consistently day after day. They may work for a week, for a month or so, take a few days off, come back again and then take some more days off, for any number of reasons. Employers have found that if they can provide day care centres, absenteeism is cut significantly.
I would hope that in the future many of those businessmen who presently complain about absenteeism will understand the attraction of building into their work site day care facilities so that their employees will have a more compelling reason to come to work than they apparently have now.
Continuing in this vein, Mr. Speaker, studies indicate that the presence of day care centres improves employee attitudes towards the sponsoring organization; in other words, employee morale builds up with the introduction of day care centres. Such an increase in morale, of course, brings increased productivity.
How often have members stood in this House and argued that the essence of the fight against inflation ultimately is increased productivity? I am not going to argue that the emergence of day care centres across the marketplace in Canada will suddenly and dramatically decrease inflation. 1 will argue that widespread introduction of day care centres into the marketplace will be one of the important tools the government and private industry can utilize to help to combat this pernicious spectre of inflation which seems impossible to defeat.
In addition the introduction of day care centres lowers the job turnover rate. Those employers 1 was talking about earlier who were worried about this persistent problem of employee turnover-here today and gone tomorrow-will find that particular difficulty of doing business significantly reduced if day care centres are introduced in their particular business.
The government, of course, is not directly involved in the placement of day care centres in private industry. The member for Vaudreuil indicated earlier, quite accurately, that we do not have jurisdiction to get directly involved in the day care
Energy Administration Act
issue. That we do not have direct jurisdiction in this field does not mean that this government has not played a role in spreading day care services throughout the country. In 1980 alone, through the Canada Assistance Plan, approximately $40 million has been channelled to provinces and to municipalities to help them create and run day care centres within their respective jurisdictions. To some people that may not be enough money but I would argue, Mr. Speaker, that it is an excellent start and 1 would hope this government in future years will involve itself in even larger amounts.
Getting down specifically to the topic raised by the hon. member for Vaudreuil, I would like to indicate that Treasury Board approved of a pilot project that contemplated the creation, within the federal civil service anywhere in Canada, of three day care centres. I would like to point out this afternoon, lest there be any confusion in the minds of the members present today or to anyone who may read Hansard, that the day care centre in the Confederation Building is not one of those projects. It is an independent, separate project undertaken at the inspiration and under the leadership of Madam Speaker, but not Treasury Board, not this government.
Ah, you don't want to take responsibility for that one, do you?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the President of the Treasury Board
speechtext: The pilot project which was approved by Treasury Board has had three responses. The departments which expressed interest are Environment Canada, Energy, Mines and Resources, and Employment and Immigration. Of those three, Treasury Board approval has been given to but one, that is, Environment Canada.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: Order, please. The hour provided for the consideration of private members' business having expired, the House will now revert to Government Orders.

The House resumed consideration of the motion of Mr. Lalonde that Bill C-103, to amend the Petroleum Administration Act and to enact provisions related thereto, be read the second time and referred to the Standing Committee on Energy Legislation.

Mr. Speaker, in the few moments during which I spoke on this bill before private members' hour I began to make a point as to why I and many other members of the House, particularly those from western Canada, are today feeling the anger we do when we see the potential of Canada being so seriously hurt as a result of the

April 22, 1982
Energy Administration Act
economic and energy policies of this government. Those policies, and particularly the National Energy Program, are literally driving the Canadian energy industry out of the country.
I told you, Sir, that since the National Energy Program was announced, 231 oil drilling rigs have left the province of Alberta and, along with them, 111 service rigs. I mentioned that in the United States drilling activity in 1981 was up 26 per cent over 1980, but that in Canada it was down by the same amount.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development
speechtext: Talk about now.
During 1982 the decline will be even greater, 33 per cent below the 1980 figure.
It is down 20 per cent in the United States, and dropping.

Oil stays locked up in the ground. An estimated 300,000 barrels a day are locked up. That oil could save Canada $12 million a day. That oil would spell prosperity for the whole country. Instead, we import oil from abroad. We import it from Mexico, Venezuela and Saudi Arabia, and we spend $6 million daily subsidizing the price of that oil. What kind of madness is that? Does the ghost of Kafka walk silentfooted through the bureaucratic corridors into the minds of the policy makers?
When we have Canadian oil left in the ground, why do we subsidize the price of imported foreign oil? We began that subsidy originally so that the consumer in the east would not have to pay higher prices than the consumer in the west. The eastern consumer then, as now, largely used imported oil. Yet today Canadians all over our country are paying more for their gas than the unshielded American consumer who has had to pay world prices ever since those prices started rising. In short, we are being asked to support a wrong-headed policy.
In this bill there is a section on the petroleum compensation charge. It is presently levied at $6.30 a barrel, which translates into 24 cents a gallon at the pump. What we are being asked to do is authorize the government to raise it to double that amount, 48 cents a gallon at the pump, so that foreign producers benefit when our own oil sits in the ground.
That is not all. We are also being asked to authorize a levy of $1.15 per barrel, or four cents a gallon at the pump, so that the government can continue to finance a misguided policy of Canadianization through nationalization, not through the private sector. The present gas price is $2 per gallon. How much higher can the price go? Do Canadians realize that of that $2, $1.35 goes toward taxes? That is a full 67 per cent of the price consumers pay for gasoline. What more clearly demonstrates the suffocating intrusion of government at all levels of our economy than that devastating statistic? I will repeat it; 67 per cent of what the consumer pays for gasoline goes straight to government through taxes.
In 1980 the present Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) berated the Progressive Conservatives for suggesting an 18 cents a gallon excise tax increase on gasoline, yet in 1981 federal taxes
increased by 32 cents. Surely there are some supporters of the government opposite whose self-respect cannot swallow that. Surely they realize that it breeds in people deep political cynicism, and surely hon. members opposite will have to pay a political price for this mismanagement. In short, the people of Canada keep on paying more, not because the oil companies want them to but because the government demands it.
The increase to the consumer which is the result of the National Energy Program and the federal-provincial pricing agreements has been dramatic. That increase has not gone to the oil industry. What the industry faces now is diminished returns. Last year's cash flow declined by 35 per cent, and earnings declined similarly. Now Shell Canada Resources Limited informs us that investment in western Canada will be $2 billion per year less than in the pre-NEP era. This is not the road to the goal of energy self-sufficiency; it is the road to economic disaster.
Recognizing that the oil industry is in trouble, the Alberta government recently announced royalty rollbacks of $5.4 billion over the next five years. In 1982 alone Alberta will forgo $530 million in royalties. It will further grant $505 million in royalty tax credits to small producers and $250 million to well servicing companies. That is a responsive and positive act by the provincial government.
Now we ask, why does the federal government not take corresponding steps to spur the industry, for example, by lowering industry taxes? I am not asking the federal government to line the pockets of oil producers; rather, I am simply asking the government to look at an industry which is truly troubled, upon which the prosperity of my province depends, and because all provinces are intertwined in today's economy, the prosperity of all Canada is being affected.
The money we spend on imported oil is money which leaves the country. The capital which is attracted elsewhere is capital which leaves the country. This cash outflow keeps the dollar low and interest rates high, and high interest rates mean houses which have to be given up when mortgages come up for renewal and businesses which have to close down and go into bankruptcy. In Alberta, business bankruptcies last year were 39 per cent higher than in 1980. They are higher again this year. Unemployment is rising also. It now stands at 6.7 per cent, when a year ago it was 3.5 per cent.
A few days ago the Edmonton Journal reported:
Alberta's slumping energy industry has cancelled job offers to 27 engineers graduating from the University of Alberta.
Last year 90 per cent of engineering graduates found jobs upon graduation. This year only 50 per cent will be successful.
The Journal commented on the Alberta royalty rollback, and stated:
What started in 1980 as a federal grab for resource revenue from Alberta through the NEP concluded this week with a federal win. Alberta did not give in to industry by retreating on royalties; it gave in to Marc Lalonde.
April 22, 1982

That is the kind of statement that is finding growing empathy with Albertans. That is a fact of political life that I find extremely worrisome, for it is this fact that is provoking the spectre of separatism.
In the near decade that I have been a member of the House of Commons, I have warned of rising alienation in the west. On February 26, 1973, I spoke of western resentment at being treated as a hinterland by Ottawa. I spoke of the western desire for "an even break". I spoke of the need for economic justice. I said "Western development must transcend politics."
That is a theme that I have pursued during the years. But politics has apparently triumphed over good sense, for public policies have not recognized the reality of the new west. Western needs have not been met and what is worse, public policies are crippling our development, dashing the legitimate hopes of those who believe in free enterprise and know that free enterprise was the way in which the west was first built.
On December 19, 1980, I warned the House that the flame of separatism was growing in the west. I pleaded for tools for western MPs to fight this threat. We did not get any. Again, on June 8, 1981, I returned to the subject. I urged the government "to review its policies before it is too late." Otherwise, separatism might become a viable political force. I warned, that "a great collision of forces is coming unless a new spirit of accommodation is injected into policies and on-going negotiations."
If hon. members opposite will not listen to me, would they at least listen to one of my constituents, Mr. John Allen, who has written to me. His is one of many, many letters of anguish that I have received. After asking why a government that has practically ruined the oil industry in western Canada should now be allowed to nationalize the same industry, he writes as follows:
The intelligent choice of remaining one strong nation seems to be irrevocably lost through a mismanaged or maybe cunningly mismanaged federal government that has all regional areas at each other's throat, and who will probably never really trust each other again.
If I was the only person who thought this way you might say I was a crackpot, a radical, or someone suffering from paranoia, but nearly everyone I talk to who cares about the west or even Canada as one nation is angered and concerned and at a loss to know really where to turn for help, or what to do to help ourselves.
When Liberal members opposite spoke in the House concerning the threat of separatism in Quebec, the federal government took them very seriously. The government responded and gave Quebec MPs the tools to fight separatism. Why will those very Quebec members, who understand all too well the meaning of separatism, not respond to the demand for government policies that will stop the growth of separatism in another, equally precious, region of our country?
I urge members, and the government, to listen when I say that separatism is on the verge of becoming a viable political force in western Canada. The clock has moved to within a few minutes of midnight. I urge members to rise above partisanship and recognize the danger that confronts our nation. There is a separatist government in Quebec and a separatist party is gaining credibility in the west. This is no time for scoring cheap political points. This is no time for the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Lalonde) to be accusing western MPs of feeding western separatism. Together, we need
Energy Administration Act
to fight that growing force. We need your help. The Canadian dream is threatening to become a nightmare.
How hollow will the Constitution events of the past weekend appear in history if the return of the Constitution to Canada is followed by the corrosive growth of separatism. Energy policies that promote growth, development, jobs and an economic future for everyone are essential. This energy bill penalizes incentive. We must replace it with energy policies that promote incentive. Give us those tools, and western separatism will never have a chance.
I close, Mr. Speaker, by telling you I am not going to give up on Canada. This country is too great. I have too much invested in Canada. My great-grandfather came to this country from Ireland and I am not going to dismiss the heritage that I have received because of problems-problems that come not out of our country but out of the government that is currently administering-and, I say advisedly- mismanaging this great country.
How dare this government continue. We want to achieve the potential that Canada has as we enter the final years of the twentieth century in a new era of technology which could be the instrument to unite and develop this great country.
What we need is a sense of direction, a desire to rebuild, a sense of self-esteem, of our worth as Canadians. We need the tools and the energy which will help us build, not destroy one another.
Hear, hear!

Mr. Speaker, I welcome the opportunity to enter this debate today and comment on the National Energy Program. The effects of that program are far-reaching. They extend far beyond any previous government programs of taxation of the consumer and the oil industry as a whole. It is for this reason that Canadians should look closely at the NEP and question the seemingly endless list of taxes this government is adamant about passing on to hard-pressed consumers. From the consumer who fills up his car or uses oil to heat his home, to the small Canadian-owned energy company trying to keep its head above water, the story is the same. The NEP is slowly killing off the industry, slowly but surely strangling it to death.
In the last couple of years the government has driven billions of dollars of investment out of Canada and raised taxes almost beyond the breaking point. Every time the consumer turns around, the price of gas and fuel oil goes up because of an unwarranted increase in federal taxes. Since June, 1980, consumers have been forced to accept increases of 28 cents a gallon, and through the NEP the government intends to slap on a further 52 cents without ever having to justify or explain the increase. In total, consumers will have to pay 80 cents a gallon in federal taxes, which is an incredible price to ask them to pay.

April 22, 1982
Energy Administration Act
There is no doubt in my mind the taxes outlined in the NEP are completely unwarranted. We have the petroleum compensation charge, the petroleum and gas revenue charge, the natural gas and gas liquids tax, the Canadian ownership charge, and the federal excise and sales taxes. My God, Mr. Speaker, every time someone fills up with gas or fuel oil they have to pay these extra taxes, after which there is little left in their pockets. These taxes are bleeding the consumer dry and making it difficult for him to meet his other financial commitments. They simply cannot take much more of this heavy and wholly unnecessary taxation.
We have been told time and time again that Canadian gasoline prices would be kept below world prices. They will not exceed 75 per cent of the world price. However, the present situation speaks for itself. That promise, like many others, has been cast aside. While the international price of oil continues to fall because of the oil glut, Canadian prices continue to rise because of federal tax increases. Anyone who drives across the border will see that the price of gasoline is cheaper there, even when the rate of exchange is taken into consideration. Perhaps the answer to why we have all these taxes is that it is just avarice and greed on the part of government which is trying to extract as much money as possible from over-burdened taxpayers in order to finance some dubious government programs which do not have legitimate priority or should not have been included in government expenditures. I am referring, Mr. Speaker, to two glaring examples. The first is the recent loan to Russia of some $600 million at an interest rate of less than 10 per cent to finance the gas pipeline. The other is the loan of some $47 million at low interest rates to Algeria to build, of all things, a monument. This money could have been better used to alleviate the dire straits and financial difficulties of many of our farmers. Our hard-pressed housing industry could have used some of that money. However, because of a twisted sense of priority, these two groups along with others are to be denied.
1 firmly believe, Mr. Speaker, that charity begins at home. We should make sure our own house is not wanting before we gallivant across the four corners of the world squandering the taxpayers' money to prop up countries whose ideology is opposed or even hostile to ours.
The National Energy Program is supposed to increase Canadian ownership of the energy industry to the extent of 50 per cent by 1990. We are also promised energy self-sufficiency. Those are worthy goals and hard to disagree with, and have long been supported by our party. However, the NEP has had just the opposite effect. It has done a great deal to force Canadian companies out of Canada, and in so doing push back any hope of self-sufficiency for years to come. In the last 15 months or so some 270 drilling and service rigs left Canada, taking with them the technical expertise which in the 1970s accounted for 70 per cent of our oil and gas discoveries. Many of them will not return to Canada, nor will many of the Canadian entrepreneurs. The jobs they would have created, the secondary spinoffs which are so important to the recovery of our economy, are now being enjoyed by the Americans. Mr. William Mackness of the influential firm of Pitfield, Mackay, Ross estimated that in the first year after introduction of the NEP $17 billion in capital left Canada. With a massive outflow of capital of that kind how is the oil industry supposed to be Canadianized? How is it to survive?
While this is happening Canadians are faced with a very disturbing and unnecessary reliance on uncertain supplies of foreign oil. The government seems to want to leave Alberta oil in the ground to the tune of some 300,000 barrels a day, and to delay exploration for new resources. Again I ask, what has happened to the goal of Canadianization? I believe the answer is quite simple: the oil industry is being taxed to death, just like consumers. In the last year alone the government collected $8 billion in taxes under the NEP. The hardest hit are the Canadian-owned independent oil and gas companies, the companies which are supposed to form the cornerstone of the government's Canadianization program. According to Petroleum Monitoring Agency figures, Canadian-owned companies suffered a 52 per cent drop in income in the first half of 1981. There is no question in my mind that this government is not interested in helping Canadian independent companies grow and flourish in the oil industry. Instead, it seems intent on taxing these companies to death. I ask you, where is the common sense?
I would now like to speak briefly about the petroleum compensation charge. A close look at this part of the bill shows that a program of taxation to pay for foreign oil is an ambiguous plan, to say the least. What we have here is a description of the maximum tax which can be charged to pay for imported
oil.	At present it is $6.30 a barrel, but the ceiling can be increased whenever the minister wants it to $12 a barrel. The impact at the pump for consumers is another 24 cents a gallon.
I do not believe this is what Canadians bargained for or what they want. Again there is no question, in my opinion, that the discretionary power given to the minister is dangerous. Nowhere in the bill is there any provision that ties in with what is charged through the petroleum compensation charge to the quantity of oil that is imported. As it stands, the government has the authority to charge as much as it wants for as long as it wants, and the tax is not tied to the cost and the amount of imported oil.
What the government is doing is demanding a blank cheque signed by the taxpayers of Canada. What nonsense. No individual or businessman would ever do business in this way. To top if off, as of now, the government has more than $1.4 billion in this fund. Yet by this tax the government insists on this form of taxation even with the fund being $1.4 billion in the black.
To me this is greed of the highest order. To make matters even worse, there are no assurances that the moneys raised through the petroleum compensation charge are earmarked necessarily to buy foreign oil. To me this represents fraud of the highest magnitude and is the taking of money from the
April 22, 1982

Canadian taxpayers under false pretenses, and it should not be tolerated.
I strongly protest the authority of the minister to raise taxes at will. What is needed in this bill is a statement of principles, a clearly spelled out set of principles so as to balance out and equate the level of tax collected under the petroleum compensation charge with the amount of oil that is imported. I do not believe that any government purposely goes out and plans to shut down the oil industry and create complex havoc and uncertainty.
Having said that, I find it extremely difficult to equate common sense with the decision taken by this government in this regard. The reason I say this is that the government, despite good advice from various sources from knowledgeable people all across our land has damaged our economy. It refuses to look around to see the devastation it has created.
I believe that Canadians should pay a fair price for energy while the government moves toward energy self-sufficiency. I believe this is an important and worthwhile objective. But I also fervently believe that the government, through the National Energy Program is creating chaos in the industry and is needlessly over-taxing consumers. What is equally alarming is that we are not moving toward self-sufficiency, especially when we are importing more and more oil. Not too long ago, this government defined a fair or reasonable tax on energy as anything that did not exceed an 18-cent tax. Now that definition has changed where we will be paying at least 80-cents in tax on a gallon of gas as well and an 80-cent tax on a gallon of fuel oil.
The government has introduced many taxes, but there is only one taxpayer, the Canadian people. The taxpayer can only pay so much. You cannot get blood out of a stone no matter how hard that stone is squeezed. A tax rebellion in Canada is not impossible. It can happen here.
My advice to this government is to get its head out of the sand and take a good hard look at the real world. Then, we hope, common sense might prevail again.

Mr. Speaker, every time I speak on an energy bill I cannot help but think about just how differently I see energy from the way the government sees it. When I look at it in terms of the area I represent, I think of jobs, of opportunities, of cash flowing through my community and of the spin-offs into other industries in the area, whereas the government seems to think only of energy and of the energy sector as nothing more than a source of revenue, of capital and of being able somehow to deal with the huge deficit it has built up over the years.
I take particular interest in speaking to Bill C-103 because it is one of the bills that flowed out of the hard work done during the ringing of the bells to break down Bill C-94 into workable and debatable pieces of legislation, legislation which could be looked at and considered in some kind of a reasonable format where we could talk about the various elements of it in some detail instead of having to look at the matter in the omnibus fashion in which it was presented to us a few weeks ago. I have a few objections to this bill which stand out in particular. The first one has to be taxes. This bill is really nothing more than a
Energy Administration Act
tax bill, a grab for revenues. It is a grab for revenues at a time when people all across Canada are losing their jobs, their homes, their businesses and anything that would allow them any opportunity to pay taxes. But the government is increasing taxes.
The second area of concern that I have with this bill is that more money is being collected through the petroleum compensation charge than is necessary. The government is taking a greater share of taxes than it really needs.
There is a third area that I do not like about this particular bill and that I do not like about this particular government. A certain trend and approach has been developed by this government in the way it governs. We have seen so much ministerial discretion, and so much done by order in council and so much done behind closed doors. As we study this bill we find that is the format, the approach, the method and technique used in this particular bill.
Looking at the first concern I have, the matter of taxes, we find at the present time the petroleum compensation charge already being levied is around 24 cents a gallon. Bill C-103 will allow the government to almost double that amount, to increase the charge by almost another 24 cents a gallon.
At 24 cents that amount is half what was originally intended in the legislation that was before the House before we started ringing the bells. Already the government has taken the time to pause a little because it knows there will be a little more public scrutiny. The public will have a chance to look at these particular taxes. Therefore, from the first piece of legislation which the government introduced at the time of the bells until now it has cut the taxes in half.
The Canadian ownership charge, the charge that was used to enable Petro-Canada to buy Petrofina, has already been levied on consumers at the rate of about 4 cents a gallon. That amount is also to be increased. But once again it has been cut by roughly half of what was originally brought forward in Bill C-94, the bill which caused the ringing of the bells. This Canadian ownership charge when it was introduced was introduced by the minister with the promise that it would be in effect for about a year and a half only. If we take a good look at Bill C-103, we find that there is no mention of a time limit on the Canadian ownership charge. In fact, all indications are that this particular fund will be increased. It is to become the minister's cookie jar. it will be his source of funds to spend at his own discretion. It will be applied in various circumstances to make purchases, to buy shares, to buy bonds, to buy little oil companies and service stations, and to buy any number of things the minister sees fit to buy. He will have his own little fund to use.
Another tax with which we have been dealing is the oil export charge. It can now be set under the jurisdiction of the bill without the advice of the National Energy Board. Once again it is an example of taxes being set behind closed doors or

April 22, 1982
Energy Administration Act
without the advice of a legitimate board. The National Energy Board will no longer provide advice on this particular charge. The oil export charge and the revenues it brought to the government were promised to be split with the provinces. Producing provinces were to receive one half of those revenues. But when we look at Clause 11 of Bill C-103, we find no mention of that fact or no guarantee and, once again, the terms of the taxes are to be set by order in council.
Let us look at some of the taxes imposed upon petroleum products in the country. There is the petroleum and gas revenue tax which is approximately 12 per cent on all oil and gas production. There is the incremental oil revenue tax which amounts to about $2.50 per barrel this year and will increase next year. There is the federal sales tax on gasoline which is now running at 9 per cent. It is applied the moment a gallon of gasoline leaves the refinery. In addition, there is the excise tax on gasoline of about 1.5 cents per litre. All the way through we see nothing but taxes on taxes on taxes.
In Bill C-103 the government also saw fit to remove parliamentary debate in a large number of areas. Now we will have taxes set by order in council, as I have mentioned, and taxes set behind closed doors, taxes without debate, taxes without discussion by parliamentarians and, therefore, taxes without input from Canadians. There is an exception, that is, the fact that any "major" purchase can be debated in the House of Commons. It sounds good until we start looking into it carefully. Then we discover that the debate is limited to three hours- the minister speaks for 40 minutes, our critic speaks for 40 minutes, and then the critic of the New Democratic Party. What chance will I have as a backbencher? I represent an area which is dramatically affected by energy, but what chance will I have to speak on tax reforms or pieces of legislation which will come before Parliament? It will not be very much. There will not be much opportunity for input. In other words, my constituents will have very little opportunity to have their concerns expressed because we are limited to three hours of debate.
Another item which I find interesting about the bill is that all taxes and charges will be retroactive to October 1980. We find that taxes have already been collected for various charges and levies throughout the bill without legislation. Bill C-103 is the legislation for that but it is a retroactive piece of legislation. If we look at the total federal government tax take, we find that at present it is running about 60 cents per gallon. If we break that down to litres, which everyone is forced to buy in now, it works out to about 13 cents per litre. If we assume that we are working on about 39 cents per litre for gasoline, about 13 cents or roughly one third is being consumed by federal taxes. Approximately one third of the cost at the gasoline pumps is federal taxes.
The government's reason for collecting these taxes is most disturbing. It is motivated by a greed for more revenue in an attempt to cover the deficit which it has allowed to build up over the last decade. It is an attempt to obtain more money to support absurd spending habits, such as loans to Russia, monuments in other parts of the world, and building sewer systems in cities which are sinking. The government is not
interested in taking any of this revenue and putting it to work in the country. It is not interested in using it for exploration, the development of the industry, or to create jobs. We know that if one rig is operating it employs approximately 30 people.
A short time ago I spoke in the House on an energy bill. 1 talked about the number of wells which will be developed in the United States next year. When I commenced my remarks I mentioned that the government has been collecting more petroleum compensation charges than necessary. I will briefly expand on that subject. Statistics Canada figures indicate that the government has been collecting $5,688 billion in oil import compensation. If we review that figure, we find that the government only paid out $4,265 billion. Those mathematics indicate that there has been more collected than expended by $1,423 billion. If that figure is broken down to a tax per gallon, the result is about 7 cents per gallon too much tax. If that is broken down even further and regarded in terms of total tax collected and tax surplus, it equals almost one dollar in every five dollars that is surplus. That is 20 per cent too much which could have gone back into the hands of our farmers, consumers and senior citizens who must heat their homes, drive their cars and do all those things that require the use of petroleum energy.
Why has this happened? First, it has happened because there has been a decline in demand for oil and its related products in Canada. The reason for this decline is that we have begun to purchase smaller cars and better insulate our homes. All Canadians have started to become energy conservation conscious. We have started to think in terms of how we can all personally save some energy and conserve on gas and oil. The undertaking of those conservation methods have resulted in a decline in demand for petroleum products. Canada presently imports about 400,000 barrels of oil per day. Those tax dollars which have been collected through our import compensation charge have been used to reimburse importers.
The difficulty we are facing now is that while our consumption is declining we are continuing to import the same amount of fuel. The resulting over supply affects my region in Canada very seriously because oil is left in the ground. While it is still under the ground there is no possibility for creating jobs or for obtaining revenue nor can there be any economic spin-offs throughout our region. Instead, we are creating jobs outside of Canada. Taxpayers are unnecessarily paying the same amount for these imports, while money is spent outside of Canada at a time when we are creating no wealth and no opportunity to collect taxes from those people who are working and spending money. We are left with nothing.
