Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to participate in the debate on Bill C-103, an act to amend the Petroleum Administration Act. The main act which this bill seeks to amend was passed by the House of Commons seven years ago almost to the day, in April of 1975. It had three stated purposes, according to the government. The first was to impose a charge on exports of crude oil and petroleum products in order to discourage such exports from being sold at bargain basement prices and, of course, to raise revenue for Canadian energy goals. The second purpose was to provide compensation for the importation of petroleum. Eastern Canada was then, and it continues to be now, highly reliant on foreign supplied petroleum which is much more expensive than domestically supplied petroleum available in other parts of the country. Thus, the government instituted a means of subsidizing the cost of foreign petroleum so as to standardize prices to the consumer from one part of the country to another. Finally, the act sought to regulate the price of Canadian crude oil and natural gas in interprovincial and in export trade. The government apparently did not want different prices being charged by different producing provinces or companies for the same petroleum products, either within Canada or for export.
Later, in April 1978-and April seems to be a special month for this act-the Petroleum Administration Act was amended to allow certain types of Canadian oil to receive the same compensation as foreign oil. I am referring, in particular, to oil from the Syncrude and Suncor plants in Alberta. The government was authorized to impose a special levy to a maximum of $1 per barrel on all oil produced in Canada or imported into Canada to pay for the subsidy.
Now we have yet another bill to amend the Petroleum Compensation Act. In fact, the government is proposing to overhaul completely the Petroleum Compensation Act. Its title is to be changed to the "Energy Administration Act". Of special concern to myself and to other Progressive Conservative members of Parliament and, I believe, to Canadians right across the country, are two particular provisions devised to authorize the federal government to impose hefty energy taxes on consumers which are already being collected without legal authority. The first one is the petroleum compensation charge. It is currently being levied at $6.30 a barrel, and that charge has increased the price of gasoline at the pump by no less than 24 cents a gallon. Only about $1 per barrel or four cents a
gallon of that amount has yet received legal authority. According to experts, every time the price of oil goes up $ 1 a barrel at the wellhead, we get a corresponding increase at the pump for gasoline of about four cents.
The bill before us seeks to provide the required authority retroactively. The present government is making a practice of this. It announces an energy tax and then immediately collects it. Normally, the tax is effective immediately. But the government does not get around to seeking from Parliament the legal authority for the increase until weeks, months, or, in some cases, years afterward. In effect, Canadians are paying huge energy taxes which the government had no legal authority to impose. As if such a provision were not offensive enough, the government is seeking in this case to give itself a blank cheque to increase the charge even higher to a maximum of $12 a barrel or about 48 cents a gallon at the pump. That is one hefty tax.
The second hefty energy tax contemplated in the bill before us concerns the so-called Canadian ownership charge. It was instituted to raise money from the Canadian consumer for Petro-Canada's purchase of Petro-Fina. In this case, the levy is $1.15 a barrel, or about four cents a gallon at the pump. In a few minutes I hope to have occasion to talk about the purchase by Petro-Canada of Petro-Fina. However, for the moment let me just say that what we have here is a scandalous, ill-disguised tax grab by the Trudeau government at the expense of the average Canadian.
In the last election, the Liberal party promised the electorate, "Vote Liberal and energy prices will come down. Vote Liberal to keep energy prices down". That was the slogan. Since then, the government has imposed a bewildering array of energy taxes, a total of 14 separate ones to date. Fourteen separate energy taxes have been imposed on the Canadian consumer since the Trudeau government was brought back into office in February, 1980. By the end of 1982, gasoline prices are expected to be twice as high as those in effect when the Liberals conspired to defeat the Clark government for proposing to raise gasoline prices by only 18 cents a gallon. The Liberal party and the New Democratic Party in the House of Commons conspired to defeat the Clark government on the shallow and transparent grounds that the Clark government was proposing an 18-cent a gallon increase in the price of gasoline. Yet, by the end of 1985, the price of gasoline will be three times higher than that charged when the Clark government was in office.
At the time of the defeat, the price in my home town of Charlottetown for regular unleaded gasoline was $1.26 a gallon. The date was December, 1979. The price was pretty much the same for the same product in cities of varying size across the country. The price today is $2.25, an increase of 99 cents a gallon. A full 60 cents of the 99-cent increase is directly attributable to federal energy taxes. I would be the First to admit that some of the increase is the result of provincial taxes. Some is the result of the increased return to the

industry. There are road taxes, all kinds of things lumped in. The bottom line, though, is that we have had a 99-cent increase in the price of gasoline since the February 1980 election, of which 60 cents is directly attributable to federal energy taxes. Former finance minister John Crosbie's 18 cent a gallon increase looks very good today by comparison.
In the same vein, the price of home heating oil in Charlottetown at the time the Clark government was defeated was 74.2 cents a gallon. Again, that was roughly comparable to the price for the same product in other cities across the country. Since then the Trudeau government has pushed it up to $1.40 a gallon, an increase of 66 cents, again largely because of federal taxes.
This government's shameless imposition of steadily heavier energy taxes after winning an election on a commitment to keep energy prices down has been the greatest betrayal of the Canadian people in the history of the country. The closest parallel was the introduction of wage and price controls by the same Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) within months of winning the 1974 election on an equally categorical commitment against controls.
I need not remind you, Mr. Speaker, that the Crosbie budget energy tax on which the Trudeau party defeated the Clark government did not apply to home heating oil, only to gasoline. The Liberal Party in the February 1980 election deliberately led people to believe that somehow the 18-cent a gallon excise tax applied equally to oil and gasoline. It did not. What is more, the Crosbie budget proposed an energy tax credit for low and middle-income consumers.

I doubt that many of them would be returned, Mr. Speaker.
Canadians have a right to ask what they are getting in return for the burdensome energy taxes imposed on them since the last election. They can be forgiven for having no confidence in this government's capacity to use the revenue wisely. Indeed, it has made a complete hash-I do not think that is an exaggeration, Mr. Speaker-of energy policies in the last decade. No country in the free industrialized world has adjusted more slowly or more ineptly than has Canada to the formation of the OPEC cartel in 1973. We have had a whole decade-just short of that by a year-to adjust to the formation of that cartel based in the Middle East to force up quickly, energy costs without much forewarning. But Canada has dithered and procrastinated, and it has refused to take the steps necessary to adjust to the new reality.
Contrast Canada's performance vis-a-vis the 1973 OPEC cartel formation with that of Japan, for example. Japan has practically no capacity to generate energy. It is 90 per cent dependent on energy supplies from abroad. Yet by steadily adjusting to higher world energy prices from the very beginning-it did not wait a decade, it began immediately-Japan has kept its economy buoyant. Canada, which was self-reliant in oil production as recently as 1974, is now a net importer of oil, largely because of its sluggish response to the OPEC cartel.
As recently as 1974, this country was self-reliant, self-sufficient in oil. Our recent scramble to bring energy prices in line with economic forces throughout the world is causing enormous dislocations, one of the most serious of which is near
run-away inflation. At a time when we are wrestling with 12 per cent inflation in Canada, Japan enjoys a rate of only 3.1 per cent.
The Clark government tried to make up for the failure of the Trudeau government to protect our country's interests against the stranglehold of the OPEC cartel between 1973 and 1979. Recognizing as it did that the Canadian government did very little between 1973 when the cartel was formed and 1979 when the Progressive Conservatives took office, the Clark government did what it could to catch up for lost time. The defeat of the Progressive Conservative government, followed by two years of wrangling with Alberta over an energy agreement, further set back Canada's goal of energy self-sufficiency based on a realistic energy price structure.
The government's ill-conceived Canadianization policy threatens to put us out of the running altogether. One of the unfortunate aspects of the debate on Canadianization is that somehow the word itself has become debased. All of us are in favour of Canadianization. All of us are in favour of getting more control over our resources and our energy capacity. None of us revels in the reality that much of our resources are controlled by other countries, principally the United States. So, of course, there is virtually unanimity in this House that we should take certain steps to patriate our energy industry. The question is, how to do that. This government, through its ineptitude, has retarded that process by bringing the industry itself to its knees. The government's ill-conceived Canadianization policy threatens to put us behind, rather than ahead, in patriating our energy industry.
As long as the government insists on buying up existing oil companies at the expense of encouraging new resource exploration and development in Canada, we will continue to fall further and further behind. Too much of our scarce investment capital is being used to buy up existing companies, rather than encouraging companies to go out and explore, develop and create new energy wealth for us and for sale in international markets. I ask, what earthly purpose is served by buying up service stations, as the government did with the Petro-Fina purchase, when that action adds not a drop of oil to domestic supplies? It knows that it passed the 18 cents per gallon point long ago.
This bill proposes that the government's tax grab, under the Liberal Party's policy, be higher than the current sky high levels. It seeks to approve retroactively the special compensation charge that the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources imposed when he was unable to come to an agreement with the province of Alberta. It is no wonder that the minister was not able to come to any agreement with the province of Alberta. It is hard to figure out how he could ever come to much of an agreement with anybody. It is obvious that he has applied his usual method of confrontation and bulldozing ahead. His lack of reason is evident in the way he negotiates things. That is why he has had such difficulty with the Alsands project, a project which means so very very much to the people of Canada. The Alsands project is not just an Alberta project; it
is a Canadian project, one which would put Canadians to work right across the country.
In my riding of Simcoe North, Fahramet Limited, which produces refractor tubes used in refineries, has had to lay off people because the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources cannot come to an agreement with anybody.
In December 1979 the price of gasoline in Toronto was $1.18 per gallon. By December 1981 the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources, under the Liberal party's high energy tax policy, managed to get it up to $1.89 per gallon. That is an increase of 71 cents per gallon in two years when the Liberals promised the increase would be less than 18 cents per gallon.
My friend who put gas in the tank and I chatted a little. He had been to Florida for a holiday. He told me that he paid as little as $1.13 per gallon on that trip, and that is the Canadian gallon, Mr. Speaker. Under the great policies of the Liberal party, it has managed to get the price of our gasoline up to $2.00 per gallon.
You will remember that during the last election campaign, Mr. Speaker, the Liberals focused on the figure of 18 cents. For a moment I should like the House to focus on the figure 16 cents. In a little over two years the Liberal Party has been responsible for 16 increases in the price of gas. I am not asking you to focus your attention on the kind of increase, Mr. Speaker-we know they amount to 71 cents in two years-but to focus on the number of times the price has been increased. There have been more increases in the price of gasoline under the Liberal Party than there have been budget retreats by the Minister of Finance (Mr. MacEachen). He is off again, consulting. He has made five retreats since December 13 and we can count the number of changes to be in the thirties.
There is something to be said for the Liberal party and the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources, Mr. Speaker-16 increases in a little over two years from a party which said it would never increase the price of gas by 18 cents!
In December 1979 the price of heating oil was 69 cents per gallon in Toronto. Under the Liberal Party, the party which lied its way across Toronto, lied its way across Ontario, lied its way across Canada, the price has gone to $1.22 per gallon, an increase of 53 cents per gallon in the two years since that party promised it would be less than 18 cents per gallon.
In the election campaign the Liberals talked about 18 cents per gallon with great glee. They did not focus on a matter called the refundable energy tax credit. In the budget which the Liberal party criticized and complained about and said would never do, the energy tax credit paid to Canadians to cushion the impact of high prices on low and middle-income families would have been up to $80 for each adult and $30 for each child under 18. The credits would have been refundable so that families who paid little or no federal tax would have received the full benefits. That was for families with an income of $21,380.
The Liberal party, which said it would not tax Canadians 18 cents per gallon, for once may be said to have told the truth- if you consider that it did not stop at 18 cents. I see you are
April 22, 1982

nodding your head, Mr. Speaker. That is actually what happened. They told the truth. In that one instance they did not stop at that 18 cents but went on and on and on. The Progressive Conservative policy, which it laid out truthfully, was to give people an energy tax credit, but the Liberals said "We won't raise the price of gasoline." They never said anything about heating oil, they just went ahead and did it.
I am pleased to take part in this debate for a very good reason, Mr. Speaker. During the 1979-80 campaign my Liberal opponent waxed long and loud throughout Simcoe North with respect to the price of gasoline and the tax on gasoline. He came to my riding from metropolitan Toronto. We did not call him a parachute candidate; he had a hobby farm in the area for several years and used to come there on weekends. We wondered why he did not go back to his riding in Scarborough on the weekends, but all that became very clear when we realized he was elected in 1974 on the Liberal platform of: "We will not put in wage and price controls." I ask you, Mr. Speaker, if you had campaigned in 1974 on that platform would you want to go back to your riding on weekends? Obviously not.
His name was Allan Martin. He was very plain about what the Liberal Party was and was not going to do. He put it right on the record. The Liberals will not sock it to the ordinary taxpayer by imposing an 18-cent excise tax on gas, he said. He was right; they did not stop at 18 cents. Two more increases and they will have a total of 18 increases, let alone an 18-cent tax. So Mr. Martin trooped around Simco North saying he was concerned about the effect of this 18-cent excise tax on northern Ontario. He said that area was attempting to promote industrial expansion, revitalize the economy and provide needed jobs. Isn't that heavy? Isn't that something? That Liberal candidate went across Simcoe North promising that they would not increase the price of gasoline by 18 cents. "Not us, we won't stop there", is what he should have said. Well, he is still in the riding, fortunately, although I do not see much of him anymore. 1 kind of liked passing the time of day with him when I got the chance, and we could talk about the 18 cents. How is the 18 cents going, Allan? Does he feel as strongly about it now as he did then? This is kind of amusing. He had a little symposium after the last budget-can you imagine that-inviting people to spend I think $10 for lunch and a look at the last budget. How could you eat after looking at it? You have seen what it has done to the Minister of Finance; it caused a disappearing act. However, he had a few people there. I am sure he was carried out on the backs of the businessmen, home owners and farmers of Simcoe North to great cheers when he told them what the budget said.
I certainly hope that he will be around come the next election, although I have to say that with some reservations, Mr. Speaker, because we were fortunate enough to have the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Whelan) in the riding last night, speaking to the Simcoe North Liberal Association. They rented a bigger phone booth this time. If that candidate can survice the Minister of Agriculture, he may be back. We run a list on this side as to which ministers we want to come into our
Energy Administration Act
ridings, and that minister is one of them. The other one is the Minister of Supply and Services (Mr. Blais), who will be in my riding tomorrow in Penetanguishene. I think he is going to help our cause considerably.
It was not just candidates in individual ridings who tried to play this game with the Canadian people. The Liberal Party, in a questionnaire put out by the Financial Post, said the 18cent excise tax was unfair, inflationary and would lead to the loss of a significant number of jobs in the Canadian economy. Well, having said that, they jacked up the price of gasoline by 71 cents a gallon and really proved it. They managed to get unemployment to its greatest height since the 1930s. They now have what they call the hidden unemployed; it is not hidden if you cannot put food on the table, but they call it the hidden unemployed. They have proven what 71 cents a gallon will do to Canada's economy.
My party lost that election on that promise, which was just as popular as the 1974 promise not to introduce wage and price controls. That promise interests me because I feel that the Liberal lie of the 1970s was: "We will not introduce wage and price controls". The Liberal lie of the 1980s was: "We will not increase the price of gasoline 18 cents a gallon." The taxes which the Liberal Party has laid on the economy of Canada in the price of gasoline have been inflationary. We have the highest inflation we have had in years. If anyone is looking for new records for this Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) to break, there is one.
I want to speak now, Mr. Speaker, about this energy legislation in a broad context. What has the Liberal energy policy done for the country? Well, they managed to increase the price of gasoline by 71 cents a gallon. They have singlehandedly been responsible for moving hundreds of oil rigs out of western Canada along with their operating personnel and expertise. That represents jobs, and not just in Alberta. Many members of my party from Ontario and the maritimes have gone to Alberta at the invitation of our western colleagues and we saw what it means to move an oil rig. Members on the other side have no idea what that means. It takes between 20 and 40 trucks of all different shapes and sizes to move one of those rigs. I do not know an awful lot about engineering, but it is quite obvious to me that when you set down 20 to 40 truckloads of steel, you do not pick up the rig and bring it back very easily. That is what the Liberal Party has managed to do for Alberta.
They talk about the megaprojects which are going to solve all their problems. Well, I think they might solve some but, good grief, you have to have one first. These tar sands plants mean as much to Ontario as they do to Alberta. As far as we in the Conservative party are concerned, this is a joint venture because in Ontario-in the ridings represented by many of the people on the other side of the House as well as in my party- there are jobs generated when a tar sands project is put into place. But what do we have? We have excuse after excuse after excuse from the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources as to why they cannot put one of those things

Energy Administration Act
together. I guess maybe it is because the minister cannot make threats. We have partners in those very valuable projects pulling out day in and day out because they cannot operate with someone who does not understand business and does not want everybody to have a job.
That reminds me, of the time when I was in the oil fields looking at a rig. A chap got off one of those trucks with dials and hoses-which my friends from Alberta understand so well, and I do not-came over and said "Doug, how are you?" I did not recognize him, but he introduced himself. He said to me, "You remember when I used to sell printing down the street in Orillia. 1 have been out here for a year now and I am making more money than I ever did or could make with my training. I am outdoors all the time and I am enjoying the job. It is going very well. I hope you fellows will do everything you can to persuade the Liberals that there is room for jobs for people from all over Canada in Alberta. We want to continue to work." But what are we doing? The Liberals single-handedly shut down the oil fields out west. While they are shutting down oil fields out west, and with that jobs are lost, what are we doing? We are importing foreign oil. What a terrific idea. You shut down what you have and you pay a subsidy to import what somebody else has. What a terrific idea. It reminds me of a story of someone who was losing money on each item that he sold and he tried to make it up on volume. Another terrific idea.
We have solved one problem, Mr. Speaker. Remember when the Minister of National Revenue (Mr. Rompkey) had all those customs people at the border checking cars coming into Canada? Well, we were able to lay them off. There is no problem now. All those Americans are not coming into Canada to get gas any more. Americans have had to hire many more people on their side of the border because Canadians now are going to the States to get gas. Why? Because of our terrific energy policy.
I do not agree with what OPEC is doing. But OPEC has an interesting concept which is as old as any economic policy. That concept is that if you have a product which somebody else wants, you sell it. For instance, you are sitting there with nothing but sand and oil. You find that you cannot sell the sand, but you can sell the oil. That is interesting. The Liberal Party's concept is that if you have a product, you legislate it, legislate it and legislate it and hope that by the time all the bureaucrats have the legislation in place, the product will be out a date, as is coal and kerosene, and extinct like the dinosaur. The thinking of the Liberal Party as to how you sell what you have stinks. It is a dinosaur energy policy. All it does is legislate. Did Henry Ford ever legislate anything? Of course not, he built things. What is this Liberal Party doing? It is legislating energy to death. What do we have? What we have is bill after bill after bill on energy. We do not have any industrial strategy, any fisheries strategy, any agricultural
strategy or any small business strategy. All we have is energy legislation.
I want to tell you, Mr. Speaker, that the last thing I want in the world is some bureaucrat trying to figure out where to drill for oil. By the time the bureaucrats get that figured out we will be on to uranium power, solar power or whatever.
I see that I am running out of time, but I know that my friends on the other side are listening to me with great interest and so I do not want to cut my speech short. Therefore, I will recap for the sake of those on the other side. I want to leave the Liberal Party with the same message the people of Canada will give them in the next election.

speechtext:
I wondered when the Liberals would wake up to the fact that all of Canada knows that they lie.
I want to conclude by saying that we are going to vote against this bill because of the terrible increase in taxes that it proposes, the burden that it puts on the consumers, but basically because the Liberal Party lied to the people of Canada.

Mr. Speaker, as I rise to speak in the debate on Bill C-103 to amend the Petroleum Administration Act, I find it quite extraordinary that the first thing the government wants to do is to change the name of the act. It is now to be the energy administration act.
In view of the problems that were created for the government by its attempted bootlegging of Parliament and of the original energy bill, I am surprised at the effort the government is making now to try to bring in a bill with the name of the Energy Administration Act. I do not know what is wrong with the Petroleum Administration Act. I noted that yesterday the minister in his remarks told us what he wanted this bill to do. He said that, first, it would establish a new ceiling for the petroleum compensation charge on refiners and importers; second, that it would establish a new oil export charge ceiling; third, that it would establish the Canadian ownership special charge; and fourth, that it would establish the transportation fuel compensation recovery charge on marine and aviation fuel used by carriers in international transportation. This bill does not sound as though it were any kind of administration bill or even energy bill. It sounds to me more like a tax bill. The four principles stated at the outset by the minister all have to do with establishing some kind of a charge for the taxpayers of Canada.
April 22, 1982

I ran across a column today written by Mr. Roy Farran, who writes a column regularly in The Edmonton Journal. In his column of April 16, he starts off with this paragraph:
Politicians would do an enormous favour to the nation if they would quit lying and start telling the truth.
Any chance of Canada's becoming energy self-sufficient before 1990 has been blown long ago.
I know because of the dates-the minister spoke yesterday and Mr. Farran wrote this column last week-that Mr. Farran could not have read the minister's speech before he wrote that column. But in reading his remarks, one might think that he had been referring exactly to what the minister had been saying here in the House. What else did the minister say? The minister continued, with syrup oozing from every pore, as follows:
Our oil and gas pricing schedule, as created in consultation with the provinces, reflects the sense of realism and fairness which characterizes our energy program. Our pricing system has three essential advantages over the regime proposed by the previous Conservative government in 1980. It ensures that prices rise gradually and predictably so that consumers and the Canadian economy in general are given time to adjust. It ensures oil pricing fairness on a national level by providing a blended price to all regions of the country, and it results in a consumer price which has been and will continue to be lower than that paid by people of most other countries.
1 think that may be the part to which Mr. Farran was referring in his opening paragraph.
Fet us go back and examine some of the minister's phrases. He said, "It ensures that prices rise gradually and predictably." He might have said that prices will rise inexorably, mercilessly or even unnecessarily. I think those adverbs would describe the price rises more accurately than the words of the minister.
He went on to talk about the government's policy of "providing a blended price to all regions of the country". 1 do not know what he meant by "blended", but we could substitute the words "equally high". The minister could have said that the policy would provide an equally high price to all regions of the country. I do not care from where hon. members opposite come; they will suffer in the same way all across the country.
The minister also said that the price would "continue to be lower than that paid by people of most other countries". That may be true. I do not know what countries the minister was counting or not counting, but he could have said that the price he was proposing would not be lower than the price proposed by the previous Conservative government to which he referred. Certainly it is not lower than the price which now exists in the United States, our neighbour to the south.
What else did the minister say? He went on to talk about the proposals of the Conservative government. I hope he knows them well. He said:
The Conservative government proposed in 1979 to pay one price to producers of oil in Canada except synthetic oil, regardless of the cost of developing and producing different types of oil. Moreover, the price was directly linked to 85 per cent of the international price, whatever the international price might be, thereby directly exposing Canadian consumers to the uncertainties of international oil prices regardless of the consequences to the country's economy.
Energy Administration Act
In other words, he said there was one price to producers of oil whether old or new oil. In the absence of the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Falonde), I ask his colleagues why that is unusual. The marketplace does not distinguish between old and new. I ask hon. members opposite to consider whether old houses are cheaper than new ones, whether old shares of a company are cheaper than new shares of the same company, whether old labour is cheaper than new labour. The answer is obvious. The marketplace attaches the same price to old as to new. For the minister to suggest that there is something wrong with paying one price does not make sense at all.
He also said that the Conservative price was linked to 85 per cent of the world price. Under this government, Canadian consumers and taxpayers-we are all consumers, we are all taxpayers-are directly linked to 100 per cent of the world price. We are now buying on the world market on long contracts. As a result of this policy and the policy to have the subsidy provided by the federal treasury, we are now in a position of exporting more than $3 billion from Canada in tax payments to foreign oil producers.
I referred to the estimates for the 1981 fiscal year before coming to the chamber this evening. The amount was $3.2 billion, in 1982, it was $5.2 billion. In the estimates for the 1983 fiscal year, the amount was $3 billion. The hon. member for Hillsborough (Mr. McMillan) earlier referred to the fact that the National Energy Program was a massive tax grab on the part of the government, put upon the poor, long suffering taxpayers of Canada. He was so right. I wonder whether he knew how right he was.
Every year Revenue Canada puts out a very interesting book entitled, "Taxation Statistics". It contains a table summarizing all income tax returns of individuals by income. I wonder whether taxpayers realize that approximately $4 billion, on average over the three years about which I am talking, represents the amount of personal federal income taxes paid by Canadian taxpayers who earned $17,000 or less. I wonder whether Canadian taxpayers realize that there are 11,300,000 people who in the last year for which statistics are available, 1978, had total incomes of $17,000 or less. This represents 78.95 per cent of all individual Canadian taxpayers. I wonder whether these 11,300,000 Canadian taxpayers, or 78.95 per cent of the total, realize that they paid $4 billion in order to subsidize the oil import program of the government.
To put it another way, we often hear, especially from hon. members to my left, about the number of taxpayers who earn over $50,000 and do not pay taxes. There happened to be 118,000 taxpayers that year who earned over $50,000. The tax grab of the government would have taken or did take more than twice the amount of taxes which all 118,000 taxpayers paid in 1978 in the form of federal income taxes.
The minister also said we would have been "exposing Canadian consumers to the uncertainties of international oil prices regardless of the consequences to the country's economy." Fet us look at the economy. First, I should like to return to the column of Mr. Farran in the Edmonton Journal,

April 22, 1982
Energy Administration Act
wherein he told us what happened to the Canadian economy. He said:
What do you think it means when Imperial pulls out a petro-chemical plant near Edmonton, when half the companies withdraw from the third oil sands plant, when Imperial disperses its team at Cold Lake, when Shell sells off subsidiaries, when oil lease sales drop by half?
Why do you think Alberta energy shares fell from $25 to $10?
I ask the government why it thinks the shares of First Calgary Petroleums, a company which I happen to know, which were selling at $6 a little over a year ago on the Toronto Stock Exchange have sold as low as $1.10 this year? Dozens of other companies have been decimated on the stock exchange.
What does that do to the economy and to investors in Canada? The drop in the value of shares on the Toronto stock exchange since the beginning of the fall-off in stock prices last year is over $50 billion. You can imagine what effect that could have had on the deficit in Canada. Try as the government might, it has not been able to build the deficit up to much over $15 billion in one year. This $50 billion which has been cut from Toronto stock exchange shares would go about half way to retiring the national debt of this country. It is a very sizeable amount.
If all these investors are losing money, somebody must be gaining. But I say that no one gains and, in fact, all Canadians are losing. The taxpayers are losing. What is occurring is that investors are unable to invest money. The provisions in the National Energy Program are so unpalatable that investors are incapable of investing. As a result, explorers in natural resources are unable to explore. A number of my colleagues have mentioned that many oil rigs have left Canada, taking with them all their related jobs to the United States where the drilling climate is much more favourable.
Although I do not have the figures immediately available, Statistics Canada released figures which indicated that the outflow of capital from Canada and the rate of increase in that outflow of capital was astounding. In fact, it is up to $18 billion during the current fiscal year. The reason for this large outflow is that investors who were investing in Canada are no longer doing so and alternatively are taking their money and investing in a better climate, such as that in the United States. In order to make Canada attractive and to ensure that our balance of payments will not completely fall out of bed, the government has forced high interest rates to be paid. It is surely a symptom of the problems faced by the Government and Canada when the rates of Canada Savings Bonds, which have been gilt-edged security for most Canadians on most occasions, have soared to 19'/2 per cent.
While the government has not been able to resolve its dilemma, and with the 1916 per cent interest rate that has caused the highest sales of Canada Savings Bonds in years- probably decades-there has been a shortage of funds which would have been available for other areas where investment is required. One such area is housing mortgages. People are not able to obtain mortgages because of the large amount of money which has been invested in savings bonds. Why would an investor want to invest in a mortgage at 17 per cent, 18 per
cent or 19 per cent when Canada Savings Bonds will give him a liquid return of 1916 per cent?
I thought the minister's remarks yesterday were about as sensible as those he made today. I was listening to the news when the minister was questioned on going into a meeting with the Alberta minister of energy. He said, after being approached by the press for a comment, "I have nothing to say at this time." He then went into the meeting. When the minister emerged from the meeting some time later he was again approached by the reporters. He said, "I have nothing to add to what I have already said." He probably did not have anything to say when he was inside the room either.
I have referred to the long term contracts into which the government induced Canadian companies to enter. As a result of these long term contracts we now have the ridiculous situation where Canadians are paying inflated prices on old contracts. While the government did not want to pay the same price for old oil as it did for new oil, it is alright for us to pay a higher price for old oil on contract while the world price for oil is falling. The situation as it exists now is that spot market oil prices are so attractive Canadian oil-principally Alberta oil, but oil in Saskatchewan and British Columbia as well-is shut-in to the extent of 300,000 barrels a day. It is no surprise, therefore, that the stock prices have been decimated. If the sales revenue of a company is removed how will it be able to cover its fixed costs, particularly its very high borrowing costs in the form of Canadian interest rates?
We know that Canadian taxpayers pay an import charge on oil. A fact which recently came to light is that New Brunswick, for example, can burn subsidized oil to produce electricity which it then exports to the United States with no recovery. Although this bill will impose a certain form of tax on exported energy, I cannot see anything in it about taxing electricity or other forms of energy which is exported after being produced with subsidized imported oil.
We have recently heard about truckers who have modified their vehicles so they can fill their tanks in Canada with subsidized oil, make their runs into the deep south of the United States and return to Canada without having to refill their tanks. This bill proposes to tax aircraft and ships leaving Canada but it makes no mention of trucks.
The transportation fuel compensation recovery charge is designed to stop aircraft in transit from obtaining subsidized fuel. However, an analysis of the bill, as I see it, would indicate that probably it will not be applied to aircraft. It is likely that some international carriers complained so much about that particular measure it was withdrawn. The compensation recovery charge will not apply to energy exported in other forms, such as electricity, as I have already mentioned.
The minister also commented that the opposition continually attacks the government's pricing system on the basis of gasoline prices at the pump. The government's spokesman never bothered to point out to the general public that the Government of Canada does not control retail gasoline prices. That is a very strange claim for a government minister to make in
April 22, 1982

1982, when his government went to great lengths during the 1980 election campaign to criticize and say what an absolutely terrible proposal was made by the conservatives to increase the cost of gasoline at the pumps by 18 cents a gallon. They said that Canadians should never have to pay that price, and all they had to do was elect a Liberal government in order to have lower prices at the gasoline pump. The minister now claims that the federal government does not control retail gasoline prices. It makes you wonder, Mr. Speaker.
My colleague, the member for Edmonton South (Mr. Roche) made reference to the emotional remarks of our colleague from Vegreville (Mr. Mazankowski). I agree that it is a very emotional issue, for different reasons, for different hon. members. My own emotion is that this is a terrible and a sad program because it is destroying the oil industry in Canada. Not only is it destroying the oil industry in Canada, but the destruction of that industry has led directly to the recession and the high interest rates of today.
We have already seen, through this government's policies, destruction of the work ethic of a whole generation of Canadians, with unemployment insurance payments rising to well over $4 billion. We do not know where on earth this will end during the current and future fiscal years.
We might ask, "What next", from a government which likes to attack these principles. As a chartered accountant, I look at what the government is doing to established accounting principles. It is not making a new attack on accounting principles. We have already heard this government state that a loss is not a loss. It started that attack ten years ago when it decided to pass a policy which meant that if one invested in a business such as a factory, and if there were sales revenues, one could deduct one's capital cost allowance on the factory from other income or any income. However, this government decided back in 1971 or 1972 that a loss created by capital cost allowance in housing was not deductible from other income like other losses. The result was predictable to everyone except the government opposite. The supply of investment in housing dried up. What happened? We do not have any supply of rental housing, and therefore we do not have any vacancy to speak of in rental housing now we have high rental rates, just because the government tried to buck the long established principles, in this case, accounting principles.
This is the same government that stated that an expense is not an expense. That was stated in the most recent November 12 budget in relation to interest payment. That was stated in many former budgets, but until very recently, concerning tax legislation, the government said that a spouse's wage paid by an unincorporated business was not an expense. We have accounting principles which state that if one pays out money to earn income, that is an expense. However, that is a principle which does not bother this government opposite.
Of course, the effect of the provision in the November 12 budget that interest expenses paid are not deductible from other income will almost totally cut off investment in small
Energy Administration Act
Canadian enterprises. How can anyone afford to borrow money to invest in a small Canadian enterprise? Let us not forget that small Canadian enterprises provide something like two-thirds of the jobs in Canada. How will anyone be able to do that when the interest paid on one's borrowings is not a deductible expense, by decree of the dictator over there?
That is the same group opposite which says that a loss is not a loss when referring to the profit or loss on sale of personal assets. If one sells a collection, or something of particular value, and makes a capital gain-a profit-that is taxable. However, if one has a loss on the very same asset, because it happens to be a personal asset, that loss is not a loss and one cannot deduct it, regardless of how it arose or whether one has any other income. The same government says that a loss is not a loss if a farmer, who is trying to build up a farm, happens to have another occupation, because then of course he is not a full-time farmer and is deemed to be a hobby farmer. Those are principles that we can afford to change.
The same government opposite, when doing its own accounts, has changed the accounting principles to say that a liability is not a liability. I see that the President of the Treasury Board (Mr. Johnston) is here, and he knows very well that his own department states that a liability is not a liability; not when it is arising out of the Supplementary Retirement Benefits Act and that liability is not disclosed in the financial statements of Canada.
I suppose these attacks on principle could be expected. But now, under the National Energy Program, this government has a new attack and has decided to adopt a new principle. It has decided that accountants do not know how to account. That change in principle arises out of the petroleum incentives program and the petroleum and gas revenue tax, or the PGRT, as it is known.
I have in my hand an accounting guideline dated February, 1982. It is an accounting guideline produced by the Canadian Institute of Chartered Accountants which most people recognize as the accounting authority in this country. I cannot read the whole guideline, but the highlighted paragraphs state:
The Petroleum Incentives are expenditure oriented and therefore should be taken into income in the same manner as the exploration and development expenditures that they support.
Further on, in relation to the PGRT, it states:
The Accounting Research Steering Committee believes that, because the Petroleum and Gas Revenue Tax is a tax on revenue, it should be charged to income at the same time as the related petroleum and gas revenue is taken into income. It should be shown as a reduction of gross revenue or an operating expense or part of government levies.
I do not expect all hon. members of the House to understand what the Institute of Chartered Accountants is stating in that bulletin, but the point is that members of the profession who do the accounting for the oil industry to know what that means and they do know how it should be handled. However, the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources did not like that idea because it would not treat those items as he wanted. As a result, he has written to the Canadian Institute of Chartered Accountants to say that it had better change its accounting

April 22, 1982
Energy Administration Act
principles and advice or he will legislate it into doing so. I have heard that from the profession, but I would like to read a little clipping from the Financial Post of April 3, 1982, which states:
The accounting profession may have won one battle with Ottawa, but lost the war. It's understood that a letter has gone to the Canadian Institute of Chartered Accountants saying the government won't prescribe Petroleum Incentives Program accounting rules, as expected, but it may reconsider the CICA's power to set accounting standards for federally incorporated companies.
Therefore, what the government is telling the accounting profession is that it does not like its principles, and if the accounting profession does not change its principles, then the government will change them. I suppose, with all the changes the government has already made to principles, which I have reiterated, we should not be surprised, nor should it surprise us, I suggest, when we look at this government's performance in past election campaigns. Some of my colleagues have referred to the 1974 campaign as a blatant example. The campaign promises of no wage and price controls in 1974 translated into wage and price controls in 1975. In 1980, the lower gasoline prices promised by the then Liberal opposition translated, for the poor, gullible consuming taxpayer, into much, much higher gasoline prices.
If we analyse the increases resulting from the petroleum compensation charge alone, which have meant price increases at the pump of 24 cents per gallon, added to the Canadian ownership charge used to pay for the purchase of Petro-Canada, which comes to four cents a gallon, we find there has been an increase of 28 cents a gallon-from those two taxes alone. This particular bill is proposing that the maximum petroleum compensation charge could amount to another 24 cents a gallon, which would bring us to 52 cents a gallon as a result of only two or three taxes.
My colleague from Simcoe North (Mr. Lewis) told us of the number of tax increases there have been. This is really quite startling. When we have a government led by a Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) who has just put his personal view on a new Constitution of Canada ahead of all government business, I do not see how these aberrations I am talking about can be surprising.
When the Prime Minister talked during an election campaign about constitutional reform he lost a lot of votes. I refer to 1972 when the Liberal Party lost its majority. In fact, it only retained its government position with a scant two seats. That was because it was talking about constitutional reform, and people were not very much interested in it. In 1979 when he again climbed on the constitutional horse he lost his government position. When he did not talk about constitutional reform in 1974 or 1980, he won. Then he brought in his ideas on constitutional reform
After the constitutional celebrations last weekend someone asked, wasn't it wonderful that we now have our new Constitution, and are we not a lot better off? I asked the questioner whether he was better off or whether I am better off. We now
have a limited number of rights because the Charter of Rights limits rights. When we did not have a Charter of Rights we did not have limited rights. We now have things missing, such as the right to own property.

speechtext: Order, please. Rather than address his remarks to the Constitution, which has been passed, I would ask the hon. member to address his remarks to the bill.

Mr. Speaker, I have been addressing my remarks to the bill for 35 minutes. I was using this illustration to show the lack of principle displayed by the government. I will carry on. I am coming to the end of my remarks in any event. I know that the constitutional debate is over, but the National Energy Program debate goes on. I hope that my reference to other actions of the government will not disrupt the Chair again.
What is clear from all of the examples I have given about principles and the Constitution is that the Prime Minister has lost touch with the views, wishes, desires and aspirations of the people of Canada. He has talked about retiring. I do not think he will, but I wish he would, and take his government with him. If he did that, we could attempt to get Canada working again. We cannot do that under the policies of the present government and a program like the current National Energy Program. If we got rid of this government we would have a chance to restore the housing industry and the oil industry. We could stop paying out billions of dollars, and it will be tens of billions before this is over, to foreign oil producers. The government says it is reducing the price for Canadian consumers. They assume Canadian consumers are not Canadian taxpayers. You can fool all of the people some of the time, but this is ridiculous. The $3 billion comes out of the pocket of the consumer of this country and goes out of this country, to the detriment of our international standing and our economy. If it could do that, we could start giving Canadians a break instead of breaking Canadians.
The policies I have been referring to are very hard on all Canadians.
I referred to the decline in the stock market. Stock prices are the way they are because values have disappeared. These companies which have been trying to do something in Canada are stuck with an enormous debt load and enormous interest rates. These are some problems we have to get resolve before we will see any changes in the economy and in the present recession; in fact it may be the present depression.
