subtopic: PRESENCE IN SPEAKER'S GALLERY OF ASSISTANT ATTORNEY GENERAL OF SOUTH AUSTRALIA
speechtext: Hear, hear!

The House resumed consideration of the motion of Mr. Lalonde that Bill C-103, to amend the Petroleum Administration Act and to enact provisions related thereto, be read the second time and referred to the Standing Committee on Energy Legislation.

Mr. Speaker, I first want to thank the House leaders who, in reaching the agreement to debate legislation on the energy question, recognized my need to speak on this matter. I also want to suggest to you, Mr. Speaker, that the constitutional debate is not over. It has hardly begun. This legislation is going to accelerate action in that area more than you think, so I intend to touch on it this evening.
May 1 say that during the constitutional debate I always spoke as a Canadian. On Bill C-103, I am going to speak as an Albertan and a western Canadian. I have no other choice if I am going to be true to the electoral base that has elected me over the last 14 years. I will speak generally rather than specifically to the principles and the application of this bill, as I perceive them to be.
The intent of the energy taxation measures within this bill is to economically weaken Alberta, if not the entire west. The energy agreement signed between Alberta and Ottawa in September last is a partial betrayal of the great vision of the west and its growth. The intent of this energy taxation bill, which results from this agreement, is to shift massive amounts of money from provincially-owned resources to the federal coffers, and second, to indirectly impose federal regulatory controls over provincially-owned resources, regardless of Sections 50 and 51 of the new Constitution.
The September 1 agreement, forced on Alberta, in my opinion, is good for the federal government and central Canada, but devastating in the short term for a once healthy western gas and oil industry and, correspondingly, the western provinces. It is an underhanded blow to the evolution and build-up of major financial institutions located and controlled in the west.
In my estimation, the federal energy taxation policies in this bill will skin off the top to Ottawa in excess of $1 trillion during the lifetime of Alberta's conventional oil and gas resources. This taxation is nothing less than a disguised royalty. When applied to heavy oils and oil sands, this skim-off will be many trillions of dollars over the next hundred or two hundred years.
The September, 1981, agreement is for a period of five years. It must then be terminated and renegotiated. If the
Energy Administration Act
agreement is extended and the tax is increased, the west will not grow as a California or a Texas in Canada, as some of us have envisioned. It will grow and mature as the institutions of central Canada dictate that it should. This is not acceptable to most westerners. The concept of equalization which is now embedded in the Constitution is a great concept, and I accept it. But over-equalization is bondage, both for the giver and the receiver, for it is better that people and capital flow together and accumulate to where there is opportunity in this vast nation. Reverse flows of people and capital in any nation, large or small, is counter-productive. That is what will happen with this legislation.
Last year, on June 20, 1981, the hon. member for Mission-Port Moody (Mr. Rose) rode home on the same airplane with me. We got into a spat over "What does Alberta want"? I wrote my views on the matter, and the hon. member for Mission-Port Moody responded, and both articles appeared in the Edmonton Journal. Let me state briefly what I said in my article. I said:
'What does Alberta want? Well, Alberta wants what all of western Canada wants-equity, leverage, some real political clout in Ottawa, economic interdependence through economic partnership. It wants to be a dynamic growing part of Canada. Some 70 per cent of Canada's land mass lies west and north of the western Ontario border. This vast area is inhabitated by approximately seven million people. Its wealth is immense. It contains vast areas of good productive land, enormous fresh water, mineral, forest and energy resources. The beauty of the landscape is unsurpassed. But this vast area is represented in Ottawa by 79 MPs out of a total of 282.
Seventy-seven from the four provinces and two from the north.
Its political clout in Ottawa is very minimal so it must depend largely on provincial governments for its leverage at the centre. Western Canada wants a fair deal on freight rates, resources, and representation in the national institutions.
As the political clout at the centre is minimal, western Canada then must use the clout of the Constitution itself-the clout of owning its vast resources. That is why ownership of resources and pricing of energy resources in particular is so absolutely vital to western Canada and Alberta.
In Alberta, we are getting an influx of 80,000 people per year and this is rising quickly.
Not any more, because of the collapse of the oil industry and the mega projects.
Alberta must build 40,000 housing units per year requiring $3.5 billion of annual capital just to house this influx. We are building a vast and complicated infrastructure, reviving old towns, building new towns, highways, bridges, airports, cities, etc. The capital required is enormous-of the order of $5 to $6 billion annually.
This vast infrastructure is being built as we convert the Alberta society from supplying conventional oil to an infinitely more complex one, supplying heavy oils, oil sands oil, gas petrochemicals and wood and pulp materials. This supply of resources is primarily for central Canada. We can build this costly infrastructure with money recirculated from Bay Street and even Wall Street, or else we can charge enough for our oil and gas to generate a capital pool which then can be used to finance this vast infrastructure.
That's what Alberta wants. That's what Alberta is doing. Financing infrastructure, house mortgages,-

April 22, 1982
Energy Administration Act
Do members in the House know that $5 billion or $6 billion of the Alberta heritage savings trust fund is invested in mortgages in Alberta?
-hospitals, complex educational institutions, research facilities, etc., with money from its own capital pool generated from its own non-renewable resources.
And why shouldn't Alberta do it? Should it mortgage its soul to the central Canadian money barons while building a superstructure to house Canadians moving to Alberta who are engaged in mega buck energy projects to feed all Canada? No, a thousand times no, the Alberta government would be accused of treason if it did not respond to the challenge. But it is not all roses-Alberta is leading the nation in rape, divorce, child abuse, alcohol and drug abuse, domestic violence, suicide, neglect and veneral disease.
-in coping with this massive influx.
Furthermore, in building these vast mega buck complexes like Syncrude, we place a severe strain, through accelerated inflation, on Alberta's conventional industries such as agriculture. Significant amounts of generated capital from oil resources must be used to effectively cope with these problems and permit other industries like agriculture to cope with the capital shortage, high interests rates, competition for services imposed on them by the mega buck projects.'
That was in June, 1981. Then the hon. member for Mission-Port Moody responded to me. What has happened since I wrote that article? Well, the Ottawa-Alberta energy agreement was signed on September 1, 1981. Then the Cold Lake heavy oil project died. The Judy Creek tertiary oil recovery project also died. Then the conventional oil industry went into sad retreat because of excessive government taxation and excessive royalties. Now the Alsands project has died and only awaits burial. I guarantee that there is no way of saving the Alsands project, because at today's rate of financing $13.5 billion, you would need $40 per barrel just to pay the interest rate on that money. It can only be financed by government financing. I do not know where the federal government is going to find $7 billion or $8 billion to finance Alsands. I do not see the Alberta government doing it. It needs every billion dollars it has to deal with its own conventional oil industry. If Alsands is to be saved, the federal government had better think of where it is going to find $7 billion or $8 billion to save Alsands. This is a sad retreat on all fronts effectively, affecting literally all aspects of the Canadian economy, increasing unemployment and deepening the recession. I say it is economic madness. Mr. Speaker, the federal government's formula for forced redistribution of the wealth of the nation has interfered massively with the Canadian process of wealth production in Canada.
We will be reaching something like a peak of all three levels of government taking 45 per cent of the gross national product this year. That is just too high. This energy agreement, manoeuvred and spawned between a single province and the federal government, sets in motion a new process for federal-provincial co-operation and accord. This is a dangerous precedent. Energy is vital to all of the nation, in every province; and the final agreement should have been ratified simultaneously by all provinces. One can ask why. Mr. Speaker, it is because every provincial government uses oil products, such as gasoline, as a massive source of taxation, as the minister indicated in the last few days. As we know, in Quebec alone the taxation on a gallon of gasoline is some 72 cents. Every government in Canada feeds massively on this industry in terms of taxation.
This agreement and the energy program of the federal government has spawned a new movement of dissent and anger in the west. It is real and gathering momentum, and at times it is scary. There are other directions and moves which are fomenting at this time, and it is appropriate to ask what the west wants. What does it want? It wants unity without bondage, justice without bias and opportunity without begging. The NEP and the energy security legislation has hurt the pride, enthusiasm and optimism of the west. The west wants constitutional protection against the repetition of this type of federal government policy and increasingly will be asking for it. The energy agreement will increase western tensions and demands, and I say again constitutional changes will be demanded, as they are being demanded now.
The Constitution has been patriated. That was a magnificent accomplishment. The fundamental rights of Canadians are entrenched. That is a remarkable accomplishment. A formula for constitutional amendment is entrenched. In my estimation it is a formula which will centralize powers even more. With the patriation of the Constitution the vision of a new nation is before us all, and we can build a nation of equality, diversity and regional balance. If we do not, then the very constitutional weapons and powers we have patriated will move this nation toward regional tension and instability.
The National Energy Program has impacted on Canada at a most inopportune time because the next several years will be a difficult period of entrenching constitutional language rights and fundamental rights and freedoms.
The political perspectives and institutional structures within Canada will, and must, change and adopt increasing regional identification.
I just want to repeat very briefly what I said on March 10, 1980, while speaking on the constitutional resolution in terms of regional representation, and particularly with respect to growth in relation to resources. I said:
This nation, Canada, will increasingly evolve, and its interdependence will increasingly grow as a co-operative quasi economic and social federation of five natural regions.
Co-operative federalism is not dead. It needs revival and renewal.
Within these regions, provinces shall co-operate and compete, shall integrate transportation and energy and other systems and shall evolve somewhat different and unique social and cultural systems. And over all, all these regions shall form the umbrella of a reorganized national Parliament.
The relationship of the national umbrella and the regional well-being, aspirations and growth will be dynamic, changing and challenging. This, then, is, and will continue to be, the essence of Canada.
Constitutional change and evolution will in the future proceed under a new format different from that prevalent over the last 115 years. Patriation itself will not be bartered and used as ransom for acceptance of a package, including the division of powers, as was done in the past. Rather, constitutional reform will henceforth be identified more with singleissue campaigns on issues such as energy. At the most two or
April 22, 1982

three issues will be considered at any one time, and these limited issue campaigns will take on regional colouration and perspective and will give rise to issue-oriented political movements and parties.
Yes, it will be an area of regional parties and regional politics imposed on the national scene with considerable fervour and force. In fact, I might say that Quebec and its discipline of political power and influence through almost total allegiance to a single party has established a precedent which will be followed in other regions of Canada. This format, enhanced by the National Energy Program, will see the Liberal Party move more than ever toward becoming a regional party. It does not have a role to play in the west so long as this energy legislation is in place. And the west is spawning a new regional party by drawing together a coalition of many political perspectives angered by the National Energy Program. It is and will continue to be increasingly moulded through dissatisfaction, anger, disillusionment and frustration as the ambitions of the west are thwarted, its desires tempered and its dynamics stifled by central Canadian government perspectives.
We need new national policies, new accords and revised political institutions at the centre. Unity will be strained as the west demands constitutional changes to influence policy at the centre, particularly policies such as the energy policy we are dealing with today. The west will not stand to be throttled again as it was by the National Energy Program. It will demand constitutional change to deal with matters like this.
First of all, it will surely demand a major Senate structural reform to give the west no less than 40 per cent representation in a much more meaningful and active Senate. It will demand changes to permit equitable, effective and meaningful representation by population in the House of Commons. It will demand a better regionally-balanced Supreme Court with some provincial appointments and, perhaps, sitting regionally at times. It will demand a restructured Bank of Canada with more regional policy input, and the gradual entrenchment of property rights in the Constitution through a provincial opting in-clause will be demanded. Much greater clarity of limitation of federal taxation of provincial resources while in transit provincially, interprovincially or internationally, as energy resources are, will be demanded.
I will say something else: there will begin to be a demand for a constitutional limitation of federal government taxation in each province, limited to something below 20 per cent of the gross annual provincial product in each or any province. Western Canada will be demanding more rapid evolution, sector by sector, of a free trade area with the United States, as was strongly recommended by the Senate standing committee chaired by Senator George van Roggen. Of course, we need to trade more north and south because of the vastness of this nation. No single federal policy direction has exercised and angered the west more in relation to future demands for constitutional limitations on the powers of the federal government than the National Energy Program and related legislation.
Energy Administration Act
In conclusion, I will say that I do not support this energy taxation legislation which has caused so much division in my part of this nation. I was very proud to be a member of this House during a most productive period leading up to the patriation of the Constitution. I think we were all proud to be members of the House during that period. But I am not proud to be a member of the House that brought forth this type of legislation which so affects a massive industry in which one out of every four employed Albertans works, directly or indirectly. This industry has been hit very hard by this legislation.
I should like to end on a less serious note, Mr. Speaker. The government's energy policy and economic direction reminds me of a little poem by an unknown author. It makes me think of the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Lalonde) and of the Minister of Finance (Mr. MacEachen), when they get up to answer questions in the House. It is very short and it goes like this:
There was a dashound once so long He hadn't any notion How long it took to notify His tail of his emotion;
And so it happened while his eyes Were filled with tears and sadness His little tail kept wagging on Because of previous gladness.
So much of the federal government's economic policy relates to happier years. A very difficult time is ahead of us. The problem of the economy has to be solved by some of the most brilliant minds of the nation. It is time that the government started to look seriously at the problem of turning the economy of the country around.

Mr. Speaker, we are in a recession that should never have happened, and it looks as though it will last longer than any recession has since the last war. It is also going to hurt more than any recession since the last war. The blame for this can be laid on federal measures which have followed, one after the other, but the National Energy Program is the straw that broke the proverbial camel's back. It is the way that the National Energy Program has been handled, rather than the down slope of the business cycle, that is to blame for this disastrous recession. The deterrents of the economies of other countries and the soaring interest rates should have been offset by the provisions of a better rate of return on the production of gas and oil and would have helped employment and increased the national income.
Practically gove is the increasing development and investment in the search for these resources, thanks to the National Energy Program, with decreases in 1981 of up to 40 per cent, and the same this year. This development and investment has now gone outside Canada, except where the government has taken up the slack.
Surely it must be realized that the grasping and clutching hands of government, which are increasingly taking their pick of the private businesses, are repeating the actions of Italy in the 1920s and 1930s, action which in Canada has resulted in

April 22, 1982
Energy Administration Act
decline in growth of the economy and, even more, is heading our country into a corporate state.
The Canadian airlines are hurting because of the transportation fuel export recovery charge which used to be levied on all international airline traffic. Now, because of a United States challenge, these charges have been dropped. Also, the government has agreed to refund to all international airlines the total charges collected over the last year. However, the government will not refund this charge to Canadian carriers despite the fact that this charge was originally conceived to place the Canadian carriers on an equal footing with their international counterparts.
Surely it must be recognized that the government has violated every single promise that was made in this regard during the 1980 election campaign. Where now can you see the cheap gas and heating oil for Canadians that it promised during that campaign? United States citizens are paying world prices for gasoline and heating oil and they know they are paying world prices. But in Canada we pay more than they do in the United States! Can the government explain this? Certainly not by quoting the price of crude oil. This does not go into our furnaces nor into our automobiles.
The government, since October 1980, in the guise of nationalism, started taking over the Canadian petroleum industry, supposedly so that Canadians could control and benefit from the exploitation of Canadian resources. This, however, was only because the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) and his colleagues want government ownership and thereby have given themselves a blank cheque to spend as much as $50 billion of Canadian taxpayers' money. That translates to upwards of $2,000 for every man, woman and child in the country.
What should have been done instead was to provide better incentives for companies and individuals in Canada to acquire control of foreign-owned companies or even provide more effective tax laws and industry regulations. Surely, if investment had been free to flow to where it could obtain the maximum return, the benefits to all parts of the country would have been greater than the costs since incurred.
It is certainly unfortunate that the government perceived nationalism as a force to be harnessed to political advantage. One wonders whether the government recognizes all the implications of its insistence that market forces can be subordinated to political direction.
Canada's interest rates had stopped well short of the American highs during the early run up, yet the Minister of Finance (Mr. MacEachen) blames high American interest rates for Canada's recession. Can he truly believe this? The National Energy Program diverted foreign investment away from Canada and domestic investment out of Canada. The budget of 1981, designed to close tax loopholes, following on the heels of the National Energy Program in 1980, strengthened the government's control over the uses to which investment would be put, that is, whatever investment remained after most had fled the country because of the National Energy Program.
The attitude of the government is that all the world is wrong not to help it in its royal right to pursue the corporate state.
The recovery of the United States from its recession used to be the springboard for Canada's recovery from its own recession. Canada's resources would be purchased by the United States-our best market, incidentally-and this would mean re-employment in forest and mining industries. But more than this is needed. High infusions of new capital are needed, but from where will it come? Certainly not from Canadian corporations; they have already invested in the United States. Those that have not invested in the United States are victims of inflation and taxes. They have no funds to invest, anywhere.
Federal intervention in the economy has brought on the recession and now, because of the state of the economy, further intervention by the government is being claimed as justified. It is a vicious circle.
The present problem is the shutdown of the Alsands project. It means the lay-off of thousands of Canadian workers; the exodus of half of the country's petroleum drilling industry south of our borders and, the bankruptcy of dozens of companies. As a consequence, $17 billion of capital has fled the country and 300,000 barrels of Canadian production per day has been shut in.
The energy program was concocted by a small group of theorists who believe state control is more important than energy production and who found a minister who shared both their philosophic bias and their profound ignorance of the way the energy industry works.
It must be realized that the tightly regulated petroleum marketing system has resulted in the federal government's subsidizing the importation of a very large volume of foreign crude oil while equivalent volumes are available but are not being produced in western Canada. This is a heavy cost to the public because the subsidies being paid go out of the country to help a foreign economy. If that money had been invested in Alsands, it would flow into the Canadian economy. Surely the government knows this could be changed to domestic production, even though it would involve drastic changes in the present regulations. By this action, which the government seems reluctant to take, money would be available for much needed job creation, which money the government claims it does not now have.
Last September, the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Lalonde) said the energy agreement would:
-provide significant stimulus for new tar sands projects.
Then his department said:
-to ensure that new megaprojects go ahead in the oilsands ... the agreement provides for generous prices on future oil discoveries-
Obviously, to quote an Edmonton columnist, the minister was totally wrong. Investors need income from present production or other tax incentives to undertake this enormous but essential project.
April 22, 1982

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
You want the oil companies to have more tax incentives.
Mr. Fret/: Ottawa controls price and the larger part of corporate taxation. Alsands will probably die unless Ottawa allows corporations to deduct investments in Alsands from other income and gives some reasonable assurance on price. The minister should meet his national responsibility by saving Alsands. He should follow the example of Peter Lougheed. Last September's energy agreement between Edmonton and Ottawa was fatally flawed, and now Alberta is paying to fix it. Simply put, and I quote the Edmonton Journal:
Last fall's agreement crushed Alberta's energy industry by taxing it to death.
A recent softening in world prices does not explain the problem. Canada is still raising energy prices toward world levels. No, the disaster was a fundamental miscalculations on taxes.
So Alberta has come to the rescue of our conventional oil and gas industry as it did in 1974 when Ottawa first grabbed successfully for a larger energy share. Now what? That question is for the minister. He has taken his pound of flesh, will he now give the needed blood transfusion to save unconventional oil, the Alsands project? Dwight D. Eisenhower said:
When shallow critics denounce the profit motive inherent in our system of private enterprise, they ignore the fact that it is an economic support of every human right we possess and without it, all rights would soon disappear.
I want to refer to four parts of that quote, the first of which is the profit motive. This government believes that it should tax industry to death. The second is private enterprise, and this government believes in socialist enterprises. The third is economic support, and Canadians have had the props knocked out from under them by this government. The fourth is that all rights would soon disappear. Mr. Eisenhower was indeed a prophet.
In Bill C-103 the government is trying to catch and make legal what is illegal. This time it introduced a notice of ways and means, and so suddenly something which was not a tax is now defined as a tax. The Canadian ownership charge is another little sneaky tax which amounts to 4 cents per gallon or $800 million a year. It is being used to pay for the purchase of Petrofina, a company the shares of which were trading at about $40 until some people who were lucky, or knew somebody, bid them up to about $80. Then along came Petro-Can to pay $120 per share. 1 would like to know who those people were who bid the shares up from $40 to $80. In the early summer of 1980 they were worth $40, and a few other oil companies were trading around that price, but now they are around $20. We can say, therefore, that had Petro-Can not bought Petrofina for $120 per share, one could probably buy a share today for about $20 or $25. The government paid about four or five times what the market shows the company is really worth.
With the taxpayers' money.

That is right, but it is not declared in the Blue Books and Estimates in a way which might alert the public to
Energy Administration Act
what is happening so that they may make a judgment. The government does not want people looking at the record, it does not want spending to go up because it wants to claim that it is holding expenditures down. So this sharp Canadian ownership charge is created in a sharp, sneaky account, outside the regular government accounts, and the money pours in. That means the minister or his appointee at Petro-Can can have $800 million per year to play with and buy more companies.
All we know is that every time we fill our tank at the pump, four cents a gallon goes into a pot for the minister and his cronies to play with. Apparently we do not have the right to know. We are only Members of Parliament, elected by the people of Canada, and that does not give us any right to ask questions about how that money is being spent or should be spent.
We also have the petroleum compensation payments, the spending part of the petroleum compensation charge, amounting to 24 cents a gallon. That money is being used to subsidize oil imported from Mexico, Venezuela and Saudi Arabia. At the same time, non-subsidized oil produced by Canadians is shut in to the extent of 300,000 barrels a day. We subsidize Pemex and Aramco while Canadian producers-western Canadians, I admit, but Canadian producers-are closed out. It is costing one company, Oakwood Petroleums, which is 100 per cent Canadian owned, a million dollars a month.
In conclusion, Mr. Speaker, I want to say that our party is going to vote against this bill.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources
speechtext: You are kidding.

I want to leave you with a quote from Andrew Carnegie, a great industrialist and philanthropist, who said:
-individualism, private property, the law of accumulation of wealth, and the law of competition; these are the results of human experience. The soil in which society so far has produced the best fruit.
This is the government which took away ownership of private property in the Charter of Rights; taxes away the wealth of individual Canadians, small businesses and corporations; renders infertile the soil for investment, "the soil in which society so far has produced the best fruit".

speechtext: Order, please. The hon. member for Ontario.

Mr. Speaker, it seems that I am having a hard time getting started on my speech tonight.

April 22, 1982
Energy Administration Act
Be that as it may, just toward the end of his speech my colleague, the hon. member for Erie (Mr. Fretz), said that we were going to vote against this bill and the hon. member on the other side said, "Oh, you are kidding." I must say that in the next election when he looks at his voting record during this terrible legislation that has been going through, he will be the one who will be wondering who is kidding whom. 1 just wanted to point that out. He had better be careful that it does not get into Hansard.
What we are talking about tonight is a catch-up bill. It is sort of a catch up, a tax grab, or whatever you want to call it. But what the government is doing is legalizing something which it has been taking from Canadians for 26 months. The Liberal government has the attitude, as the public does, of using the credit card system. In other words, charge it now and we will catch up later. The Liberals say, "We do not have to worry about it because we have a big majority. We can do whatever we want. We can run this country as we want to. We do not give a damn about the Canadian citizen."
You don't.

I am talking about you people over there.
In this bill we are talking about a made-in-Canada policy. This made-in-Canada policy is doing an amazing job of destroying the Canadian oil industry. This government has another "made-in" policy. The other "made-in" policy is the "made-in-Japan" policy for automobiles. This policy is ruining the automobile industry and it is putting 200,000 people out of work.
Oh, oh!
Hon. members over there can make a lot of noise about this, but my constituents are being hurt.
Oh, oh!
What about the steel industry and all the others?

I say to hon. members over there that they should go to Hamilton, Algoma and Oshawa and they will find out whether the people there think they are funny. Those people are unemployed because of the Liberal government and its incompetence.
Get back to the bill.

This government has also brought in a Canadian-made interest rate policy. This has destroyed the balance of industry in this country and it is also destroying every Canadian.
The legislation we are discussing tonight, which is Bill C-103, provides equalization. We are trying to talk about equalization. I would say it can better be described as total destruction of the Canadian economy through government intervention. That is precisely what Bill C-103 is. It is a clear criminal intervention by the government.
I wish the minister were here in the House. But I hope he reads what I have to say.
Where is he?

The Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Lalonde) has created sufficient havoc in Canada, so why does he not resign and give this country a chance? It is a wonderful country. It is a country we can do something with.
Oh, oh!
We do not need people yelling from the other side of this House who are saying that communism is a great thing either, Mr. Speaker.
Oh, oh!
Why does the hon. member not stand up and speak properly?
If the hon. members so interested in speaking, why does he not have the guts to come to his place and give a speech?

Let us talk about the oil export charge. This charge finally legitimizes a tax that has been imposed since October, 1980, on the Canadian people. The charge is broad enough to allow the government to raise the charge to $55 a barrel. What is left for the oil industry? There will be a negative balance. The government may increase this charge any time at its will. It can be done at the beginning of the month, the middle of the month, or the end of the month. The government does not care. It will do it any time. That is how this government operates. This export charge really eliminates the necessity of having the National Energy Board. I wish the minister of energy were here because I could ask him whether there was any purpose in continuing to have the National Energy Board keeping all those people on the payroll. Why does the minister not get rid of the National Energy Board? The reason is that the minister and Ed Clark have the whole thing in their own hands. They have eliminated the necessity of a board that would use a price, a price at which we could export without infringing upon our requirements. Why does the minister not get rid of the National Energy Board now? Why does he spend that money? The National Energy Board is just a shell. The whole thing is a shell. That is how it all turns out, Mr. Speaker. Theoretically, and I say theoretically, that 50 per cent of the oil export charge is to go back to the provinces. But nowhere specifically in that bill is the government required to give that amount back to the provinces. The provinces have no protection. The federal government can say that a product can be exported from a province, it can say how much the province can export, it can say at what price, and the federal government can impose any amount of export tax up to
April 22, 1982

$55 a barrell and not give one red cent back. The government says this is fair pool. I understand the government reduced the amount under this export charge from what was originally proposed in Bill C-94. The government has reduced the amount so that it can get the bill through the House this time. But as soon as this bill is passed and everybody is happy, the government will turn around and say, "Let us put the charge up another $100." There is no reality to the economics of the oil industry in this country.
Now we come to the transportation fuel compensation recovery charge. I wish I could get an answer to why there is a different amount for the east coast, which is $78.35, and for the west coast, which is $47.20. There is no logic in that. There is absolutely no logic. I wish I could get some explanation to that. I wish someone in the Liberal Party would explain why there are different amounts for different parts of the country. 1 note that airplanes are to be exempted and the government is going to give all the money back it charged the airlines over the past year. This government got the Americans mad enough that now this government is going to have to hand back the money. The government has done everything to insult our best neighbour. So what is the government going to do? The government is going to give the airlines their money back. It is just tokenism.
But what happened to trains? I understand the Minister of Transport (Mr. Pepin) does not believe there will be trains in the future. He is cancelling train service all across Canada. But what about trains? Why can boats, airplanes and everything else have legislation, but not trains? Is it because the trains are government owned? The train service is such a loser because it is run by the government that it really does not matter.
Then we come to the petroleum compensation charge. This is a tax that I really cannot understand. I really cannot. This tax simply subsidizes the multinationals to import foreign crude at the expense of Canadian crude. Furthermore, it discourages multinationals from going out to find new sources of oil.
Oh, oh!

Hon. members opposite can criticize multinational corporations, but they have been in bed with them for a long time. In the early days of oil development in the west, who found oil in Canada? It was not Canadians who found it, it was the multinationals. I am not criticizing them because they were fairly paid, but I am saying that we should not subsidize the multinationals to import oil and discourage them from finding additional oil in Canada, so that we will have selfsufficiency in the future for our children and grandchildren. At the present time it amounts to a charge to the Canadian public of 24 cents per gallon for fuel oil and gasoline, and a further 24 cents which the government can charge through order in council. Also the amount was reduced from $20 per barrel to $12 per barrel. It really means nothing, it is absolute tokenism. The government has reduced it from $20 to $12, but next week or as soon as the bill is passed, it will probably bring in a new
Energy Administration Act
Ways and Means motion, with legislation following 18 months later. This is what the government does now with everything. For example, it brought in Ways and Means budget followed by legislation much later. The budget of November 12 left people in confusion; no one knows what is going on. Today I received a telephone call from a gentleman on this very point who said, "What is your gut feeling about the budget?" I said that my gut feeling was that the Minister of Finance (Mr. MacEachen) is so intransigent that there is no chance he will back off; he will just pacify Canadians by giving them more time.
Turning to the Canadian ownership charge, let me first indicate that it is a real beauty! It was reduced from $4 per barrel to $1.15 and 15 cents per Mcf on gas. The government cuts back all these things in order to get the bill through the House quickly, but we must not kid ourselves-they will go back up. Let us look at what the Canadian ownership charge has done to Canada. We are supposedly talking about Canadi-anization to encourage Canadians to invest in Canada, but first I should like to refer to a Statistics Canada chart which indicates that in 1979 there was an outflow of $3,933,000 out of the country. In 1980 it went to $4,200,000 and in 1981, to $18,600,000. This is how Canadianized the oil industry has become! It is Canadianized in other countries, not in Canada. Hiram Walker is a prime example. The company spent some $500 million buying up assets in the United States. I understand that they were not the greatest assets, but the company purchased them in any event. Another example is Home Oil. Everyone thinks Home Oil is a great company, but it bought up interests in the United States. Many companies are down in the United States buying up interests there because their netback here is so bad. Last year $31 billion came back to nonresidents of Canada, at the same time that the government was paying out interest to service the debt on government bonds and on money deposits, to keep interest rates high. This year that cost will amount to $6.3 billion. Not only did we lose $18 billion in Canadian capital, we have lost an additional $6.3 billion to service the debt. The ownership charge is a fraud. It is not creating Canadian ownership, it is destroying it. The outflow is not slowing, it is increasing. The government has removed any risk-taking money from Canada and shipped it elsewhere. It brought in passive money to cover high interest government debt. It is a disgraceful situation. The Canadian ownership charge is a joke; it makes a fool of Canada.
We continue to import 400,000 barrels of oil per day. We are paying $17 per barrel, which perhaps recently dropped to about $14 per barrel, in the form of compensation. There are 400,000 barrels per day locked in, in western Canada. Perhaps the government is smart to keep it locked in, because it is not allowing any companies to develop new reserves. We must remember that new reserves are being developed in the north, in the Beaufort Sea and off the east coast. Eventually we will end up with a lot of oil, but today we are importing 400,000 barrels per day from Saudi Arabia, from Mexico-"Mexico mud" as I call it-and from Venezuela. The fact of the matter

April 22, 1982
Energy Administration Act
is that we are paying 24 cents per gallon to import it. Every time anyone in Canada fills up his or her oil or gas tank, he or she pays 24 cents per gallon for the privilege of importing oil which is not required.
The government is actually exporting $6 billion per year out of the country. In the last few minutes I have referred to $18 billion which has left by way of investment and $6 billion on interest on bonds and so on. This total $24 billion or one fifth of our national debt, so we will see the debt rise another one fifth this year. If the $6 billion had remained in Canada, it would create jobs and help solve unemployment problems which are crippling the country.
This is a serious situation with which we must deal. To put it in another way, $16 million per day is being paid out, of which Canadian taxpayers are paying $7 million. It is a $7 million extra grab of the Liberal government. This is for a Canadian-made price. On this one item, 24 cents is being paid for a Canadian-made price. We were thrown out for 18 cents and they are getting 73 cents!
At the present time when someone pulls up to a gas pump, 80 per cent of the price paid per gallon of gasoline goes to federal and provincial taxes. There are 10,000 shut-in gas wells in the west. Can one imagine how much gas that is? They are messing around on the Q & M Pipeline on the east coast. They cannot make up their mind on how, when or where to put it in. There are 10,000 shut-in gas wells which could be supplying that demand forever. They are worried that it will not be needed because of Sable Island. Let us be realistic. If there is a surplus, would it not be more marvelous if the valves were simply changed around on the pipeline and the gas shipped back to Quebec? It would reduce the cost of gas in Quebec because it would not have so far to travel from the east coast to Quebec as it would from western Canada to Quebec. We should keep it in mind as it is a very important point. The other serious reason is that due to the government grab on this, Canada is presently giving the smallest netback for producing oil of any country in the world. This is a pathetic situation which is very difficult for Canadians to understand. Since it takes so much time to read this bill, the average Canadian will not do it and will rely on us to read it for him. It is easy to read this bill because it is so bad that it can be quickly dismissed.
I refer to the Canadian ownership charge as the Petro-Canada grab. My colleague, the hon. member for Erie (Mr. Fretz) referred to the price the government would pay for Petrofina today. The most foolish thing the Liberal government did was to buy a multinational too soon. It knew how bad the National Energy Program was and the disastrous effects it would have on the industry. It knew perfectly well that $50 billion would be written off on the stock. Still, it paid 120 dollars for some stock which it could have purchased today for 20 dollars, which would have been a good deal. Not only that, it bought the wrong company. It purchased a company which would enable it to put up its service stations signs across Canada with the Liberal red maple leaf. But it did not create one job. Did it buy reserves? No. The Liberals bought service stations. They bought a distribution organization. There is not
one multinational corporation in the world which makes money out of its marketing operations, and this can be clearly demonstrated in any financial statement.
The government calls Canadian ownership Canadianization. Everywhere else in the world, particularly in those countries which respect the socialist international, this program is called nationalization. It is nationalization which is achieved by taking money out of the pockets of Canadians for which they will never receive one red cent in benefit. These companies will turn into loss leaders so quickly that we will not know what happened to them.
This is not Canadianization. Canadianization means looking back to our roots to see how our country began. This country was started by private enterprise and entrepreneurs. This is not Canadianization. It is government intervention and nationalization. Nationalization has not worked in one country in the world and it will not work here. It is a disgrace. The Canadian ownership charge, which I will call a slush fund because that is how the government treats it, does not have a beginning or an end. It will just continue to be another tax grab by the Liberal government.
We on this side of the House, as well as all Canadians, were originally told by the Liberal government that Petrofina would be paid off in 18 months at a cost of 4 cents per gallon. First, if the government had bought Petrofina at the right price it would have cost one cent a gallon for 18 months. But the government had to buy at the top end of the market. What will happen is that the government will buy other corporations which will ultimately become non-profit organizations. Also, these organizations will no longer pay taxes and help support the Canadian economy. Canadian taxpayers will have to pay for these non-profit organizations in order to keep them in business. There will be no concern for the consequences because the Liberals do not care about Canadians. Canadians are now aware of this fact, and since they are hurting right now they will not forget it.
This bill was primarily established to provide revenue for the government, and the cost to Canadians is of no concern to it. If this bill is passed, this charge could be doubled or quadrupled or changed in any way the government sees fit. There are very few defences that we have in the House to stop this bill from being passed while the government has a majority.
The Canadian ownership charge could also be called a Crown corporation subsidy. One manner in which this bill could be used is to bail out Crown corporations like Canadair. For example, in February of 1981 I brought to the attention of the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce (Mr. Gray) the fact that Canadair was in serious financial trouble. He only ridiculed me and prevented me from continuing with my point of order. I indicated to the minister that the undercarriage the airplanes it was constructing was too heavy, the plane was not designed properly and the Lear specs were not followed properly, which forced the company into serious financial trouble. I asked the minister what he was going to do
April 22, 1982

about it. What we found out was that the company went into bankruptcy. But to protect their Liberal butts, spelled b-u-t-t-s, they bailed Canadiar out for $1.5 billion. The company is not even worth $1.5 billion let alone being bailed out for that amount.
Another example relates to the energy sector and indicates what likely will happen to Petro-Canada and all other Crown corporations the government will create. Eldorado Mines commenced the Beaver Lodge mine but did not realize the small amount of uranium which existed there. Therefore, the mine had to be shut down at a loss of $500 million. That company was put into bankruptcy as well, but the Liberals solved that problem very quickly and discreetly by simply taking some stock pile from its own account-$400 million worth-and putting it into Eldorado, and then converting that to capital to prevent any interest being paid, thereby bailing out Eldorado. This is typical of what happens to Crown corporations.
This bill demonstrates the damages which could be caused by the National Energy Program. We have had enough time to see what the National Energy Program has done.
The members to my left are the ones who should be concerned about the effects of this bill. I represent union people in my riding, and my next door neighbor happens to be the hon. member for Oshawa (Mr. Broadbent). Unemployment is hurting people in our area and that unemployment was caused by too many tax grabs by the Liberal government which left too little to the industry, which therefore had to cut back and shut down its operations.
Some 253 drilling and service rigs have left Canada and 311 remain idle. Two years ago, roughly that number was being manufactured in Canada out of steel and other related products. Those products were being manufactured in Ontario and Quebec and workers in those provinces are being hurt because those rigs have left.
Furthermore, the automobile industry is being shut down because every time a job is lost in the west, two more are lost in Ontario. That is the well-known multiplier effect. The government states that it will provide great initiative through Bill C-103 and Canadian ownership to provide handouts when and if it wants. Handouts will never replace private initiative. Private initiative made this country work. Government intervention is destroying this country.

Mr. Speaker, over a year ago, on February 13, 1980, the Minister of Transport (Mr. Pepin) invited all hon. members to send him their comments on the Dorval-Mirabel issue. Considering the number of times I have raised this very important subject, I could be accused of abusing the minister's invitation. In fact, last Tuesday in the House I was hoping the minister would accept an invitation from me and from participants in the economic summit on Greater Montreal to publish the cost-benefit study on solution 6, with other studies relevant to the Dorval-Mirabel question, before the minister announces his decision this May.
Unfortunately, Mr. Speaker, the minister has refused this request, made not only by me but also by the Montreal Economic Promotion Committee, known as COPEM, which includes the Chambre de commerce du district de Montreal, the Montreal Board of Trade, and by the mayor of Montreal, Mr. Jean Drapeau, the Chairman of the Montreal Urban Community, the mayors of Montreal Island and the South Shore, the Quebec Federation of Labour, the Machinists and Aerospace Workers Union, the Quebec Travel Agents Association, the Montreal Convention and Visitors Bureau, eight major Canadian airlines, the Air Transport Association of Canada and the Societe pour le progres de la Rive Sud, under the chairmanship of my good friend Mr. Rene Delarue. All the people I just mentioned and those they represent will not be able to look at this major study before the final announcement of the minister's decision. Even the members of this House will not have a copy of the study, which, if it were immediately available, might ease the present tension and enable those with concern for this decision to remove the clouds of uncertainty that prevail today.
Mr. Speaker, I feel the ideal solution in the short term is an improved status quo, meaning that there would be no transfers of flights between Dorval and Mirabel, that the necessary improvements would be continued at Dorval and that provision will be made for improved access to Mirabel. In my opinion, any artificial channelling of traffic to Mirabel would merely discourage passengers from other regions in Canada from going to Montreal. I think it would be unwise to fragment domestic traffic by obliging part of it to go through Mirabel. According to studies by Air Canada which I support unless I get evidence to the contrary, many Montrealers travelling to the West and the United States prefer to go to Toronto by Rapidair and take advantage of the greater choice of flights offered to the Toronto market instead of making do with a limited number of departures from Montreal.
Both carriers and passengers would suffer financial losses. Passengers would have to pay more, because of the trip to Mirabel, until a satisfactory infrastructure is complete. Unfortunately, Mr. Speaker, Mirabel is nowhere near having the rapid transit system and highway network it needs to fulfill its potential and become a world-class airport. Mr. Speaker,

BANKRUPTCIES-INCREASE IN NUMBER. (B) REQUEST THAT GOVERNMENT TAKE ACTION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, last week, while Members of Parliament were taking their Easter break, Statistics Canada reported that we had achieved a
record in the month of March, a record of which none of us can be proud. In the month of March, for the first time in the history of Canada, there were more than 1,000 business bankruptcies, an increase of more than 40 per cent over the same month in 1981. This is a trend which has been accelerating over the last four or five months. There is no indication that that trend is going to slacken.
What we are seeing is not just greater numbers of bankruptcies, but a very significant change in the kind of companies which are declaring bankruptcy. In many cases these are not new companies with inexperienced management, but companies which have been in business for 25, 50 or more years. They have been very successful businesses. Let me put on record a few of the thousands which have gone bankrupt in recent months. This is but a very small fraction of what is happening from one end of Canada to the other.
A few days ago, in Winnipeg, the Victoria Leather Jacket Company, which had been in business for more than 50 years and which employed 300 people, a company owned by the present owner of the Winnipeg Jets Hockey team, went bankrupt.
In the city of Montreal a clothing manufacturing company which had been in business for 90 years, the Freedman Company, which employed at the time it was most productive and most profitable more than 800 workers, went bankrupt.
In Winnipeg, a few days ago, Wolch Limited, a clothing wholesale company which had been in business for 60 years, went bankrupt.
In every newspaper in this country one can see advertisements announcing bankruptcy sales. Here are two which appeared in the Winnipeg Free Press of April 10, 1982. One says "Liquidation Sale" in Winkler, Manitoba, one of the most productive farming communities in western Canada. This liquidation sale is of all the assets of the former New J Industries Ltd., auctioning off press brake shears, welders, presses and vehicles.
In the same newspaper there is another advertisement dealing with a "Receivers Sale" in Winnipeg for Baltic Industries Ltd., auctioning off lathes, milling machine, radial and vertical drills, and so on.
Why are these companies going bankrupt? One gets the same report when one reads the business pages of the Toronto Globe and Mail or the Montreal Gazette or the Vancouver Sun or the Financial Post or the Financial Times. They are going bankrupt for two reasons. First of all, it is because of the recession which is world-wide. Secondly, Mr. Speaker, it is because of the inordinately high interest rates.
What is happening is that companies which manufacture or wholesale goods are finding that they cannot afford to produce the goods they formerly produced, paying for the raw materials and the labour, because to do that as they formerly did would mean going to the bank and borrowing the money at
April 22, 1982

20 per cent or more in interest. Customers are not buying in the quantities in which they used to buy, not only because sales are down but because they cannot afford to pay for the merchandise when they get it. They cannot afford the kind of interest rates which the banks are charging.
As I have indicated, we have over 1,000 companies which went bankrupt in the month of March alone. For every company that goes bankrupt there are probably two, or three or four which avoid bankruptcy by going out of business, by ending the lease for the premises which they had, and by selling off their merchandise. Tens of thousands of workers are unemployed, workers who worked for these bankrupt firms, for these companies up to the time they went bankrupt. They have gone bankrupt because of the interest rates.
What does the minister say when you tell him this? He says: "We cannot do anything about high interest rates until we bring down inflation." We have lived with the government's policy of high interest rates. We have lived with Bank of Canada Governor Bouey's high interest rates for half a dozen years, and what we have is inflation at an all-time high, well over 12.5 per cent; unemployment at the highest level, the highest percentage, the highest number that we have ever had-the highest number since before World War II. That makes one and one quarter million unemployed, according to the official figures. As we know, there are another 400,000 or 500,000 unemployed who are not counted because they have given up trying to find work.
When I say that high interest rates are responsible for most bankruptcies, I am not speaking for myself alone. I am not speaking from a very radical, unorthodox position. Let me just quote a couple of sentences from the submission given to the Ontario government-similar to the submission made to the federal government-by the Canadian Federation of Independent Business. This submission was made to the Ontario government in February of this year. Let me quote as follows:
High interest rates have had their part to play in the massive increase in bankruptcies and the decision of countless other firms to simply back up. High interest rates have become overwhelmingly the most important problem faced by our member firms.

FOREIGN INVESTMENT REVIEW AGENCY-TAKEOVER OF WHITE FARM EQUIPMENT COMPANY BY TEXAS FIRM. (B) PATENTS FOR CANADIAN PRODUCED COMBINE. (C) POSSIBILITY OF CANADIAN CONTROL
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my few remarks this evening relate to a question I asked the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce (Mr. Gray) a couple of weeks ago with respect to the proposed takeover of White Farm Equipment in Brantford, Ontario, in my constituency, by TIC Corporation of Dallas, Texas.
When I first got word of this move by a minority shareholder to get total control of this Canadian firm-I was approached by an anonymous source but one who is impeccable as far as knowledge is concerned, who told me that the intention of TIC of Dallas was to take over control of the Canadian operation in Brantford, and within the next six to

April 22, 1982
Adjournment Debate
nine months phase it out gradually and then shut it down-I immediately went to the minister. I raised the issue in the House. I discussed the matter with the minister's officials in FIRA, in TIC, and the Enterprise Development Board. I put up quite a fight because I was afraid my information would prove correct. As I say, it came from an impeccable source, a very reliable source, but not from within the company itself. It came from a person who had worked with that company.
TIC protested and said that it was not going to shut the company down or phase it out. But at that time it refused to put anything in writing. The only weapon we had with which to fight the takeover was FIRA.
One other point is very important, Mr. Speaker. The White Farm Equipment Company in Brantford produces the 9700 Axial Flow combine. A lot of Canadian tax dollars went into producing, researching and developing it. I did not want the patents to go out of the country if the company itself was to go out of the country. Consequently, Mr. Nixon, the member of the provincial legislature for Brant-Oxford-Norfolk and I, even though we belong to two different parties, put up a united front. However, at Queen's Park in Toronto the Tories were quite prepared to let TIC of Dallas take over the company regardless of what promises were made, verbally or in written form.
Fortunately the federal government was wiser. It took three weeks to hammer out a deal with TIC and force it to put some of the following conditions into print. As a result of the battle that Mr. Nixon and I fought, as a result of the minister's courage in this matter, and as a result of using FIRA and the regulations pertaining thereto, we now have a written agreement by TIC of Dallas, even though it has been given the right to take over the company. The following written guarantees in legal, contractual form have been agreed to. The work force will remain at approximately 1,200 workers; all future research and development will be carried on in Canada; the employees' pension fund will be maintained; the employees' supplementary health benefit plan will be maintained; the patents to and manufacturing of the 9,700 Axial Flow combine will remain in Canada and all future manufacture of combines and combine development and combine related products will remain in Canada.
If the federal government had not stepped in, if I had not raised the issue in the House, if Mr. Nixon, a Liberal at Queen's Park, had not raised the issue, I fear that the deal would have gone through without these guarantees. Certainly if Mr. Walker, the provincial minister of industry and trade in Toronto, had his way, TIC of Dallas would have complete control today, without these written guarantees.
I am satisfied, at this point at least, that we have done everything we possibly can to guarantee the productivity at White Farm Equipment Company in Brantford. We have done everything we can to guaranteeing jobs in Brantford, even
though the workers were forced out of work for three weeks while the deal was being arranged.
Tonight, rather than being in an adversary position against the government, I am actually thanking the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce, for the courageous stand he took, and his departmental officials in FIRA for fighting the take-over in such a way as to make sure that, if it had to occur, these guarantees and many others I have not got time to include would be written into the contract.
The only thing that concerns me at this point, as far as the press release and the appendices are concerned, is that there is no mention that all this work that is guaranteed in the agreement will take place in Brantford. All it says in the press release is that the research and development and the jobs will be retained in Canada.
I sincerely hope the parliamentary secretary will be able to enlighten me on this, and guarantee that in this agreement where it says "Canada", it means Brantford and the White Farm Equipment Company in Brantford insofar as present productivity and present labour levels are concerned.

I therefore think that it is interesting to see that the questions asked by the hon. member can be referred directly to the minister and to the officials involved. We should therefore be grateful to the officials of the Department of Industry, Trade and Commerce and those who examine foreign investment because they have done a marvelous job, as the hon. member said earlier, and this has finally brought about a happy conclusion to this matter.
